title: From one cell to a whole body: layers, folds, master switch genes and regrowing

summary.text: You began as one cell with no head, no heart and no hands. Nobody put those parts in from outside. So how did they get made? In this lesson you will test how a flat strip of living cells can bend itself, with strips of spring onion in plain water and salt water. You will follow an embryo as they divide, form three layers and fold into tubes. You will also meet the Hox genes, which mark each place from head to tail, and the axolotl, who can regrow a whole leg.
summary.art: A row of five small drawings from left to right: one round cell, a ball of cells, a flat disc with three coloured layers, a folded tube with a bulge at one end, and a tiny embryo with limb buds.

intro.hook: Run a finger down the groove between your nose and your upper lip. Why is there a groove there?
intro.text: That groove is a join. When you had been growing in the womb for about six weeks, your face was still in separate pieces. Over the next week or two the pieces grew towards the middle and joined, and the groove marks the place. Your body has more joins like it. You were not carved out of one block, and you were not put together by a maker. Sheets of your own cells folded, met and joined. This lesson asks how cells can do that with nobody outside to help.
intro.art: A child looking closely in a small hand mirror and touching the groove between the nose and the upper lip with one finger.

outcomes: I can describe, in order, how one cell becomes a ball of cells, then three layers, then a folded body with tubes.
I can name the three germ layers and give two body parts that come from each.
I can run a fair test with strips of spring onion, and use it to explain how a flat sheet of cells can bend.
I can explain how a chemical signal from one group of cells tells other cells where they are, using the hand as the example.
I can say what Hox genes do, and why a changed Hox gene gives a normal part in the wrong place.
I can explain why finding the same Hox genes in a fly and in a human surprised scientists.
I can describe how an axolotl regrows a leg, and what it means that her cells remember their place.
I can give two views on a question about building bodies that scientists have not settled.

terms.meaning: An embryo is a living being in the earliest stage of growing, before the main body parts are finished. In humans the word is used for the first eight weeks after fertilisation.
terms.example: At four weeks a human embryo is shorter than a grain of rice, and their heart is already beating.
terms.art: A tiny curved human embryo drawn next to a single, slightly longer grain of rice for size.

terms.meaning: Cleavage is the first set of cell divisions after fertilisation. The one big cell divides into more and more cells, and each new cell is smaller.
terms.example: During cleavage the embryo goes from 1 cell to 2, 4, 8 and 16 cells without getting any bigger overall.
terms.art: A circle of the same size drawn four times, holding 1, 2, 4 and 8 cells.

terms.meaning: A morula is the solid ball of about 16 cells that an embryo becomes after a few days of cleavage. The word is Latin for mulberry.
terms.example: A human embryo is a morula on about day 4, while still travelling down the egg tube.
terms.art: A solid ball of small round cells next to a mulberry fruit that looks similar.

terms.meaning: Gastrulation is the stage when the cells of the early embryo move and rearrange into three layers, one over another. It is when the embryo first gets a head end, a tail end, a back and a belly.
terms.example: In a human embryo gastrulation happens in the third week, when the embryo is only about 1 to 2 millimetres long.
terms.art: A flat oval disc of cells with a groove down part of the middle, and arrows showing cells moving into the groove and spreading underneath.

terms.meaning: A germ layer is one of the three sheets of cells that form at gastrulation. 'Germ' here means 'a beginning', as in 'germinate'. It has nothing to do with the germs that make us ill.
terms.example: Every organ in your body can be traced back to one or more of the three germ layers.
terms.art: Three thin coloured sheets stacked like three dosas, labelled outer, middle and inner.

terms.meaning: The ectoderm is the outer germ layer. It makes the outer skin, hair, nails, the brain, the spinal cord and the nerves.
terms.example: Your brain and the outer layer of your skin both came from the ectoderm.
terms.art: The top sheet of a three-layer stack coloured blue, with small drawings of a brain, a hair and a fingernail beside it.

terms.meaning: The mesoderm is the middle germ layer. It makes muscles, bones, the heart, blood, blood vessels and the kidneys.
terms.example: The muscle that moves your arm and the bone inside your arm both came from the mesoderm.
terms.art: The middle sheet of a three-layer stack coloured red, with small drawings of a bone, a heart and a muscle beside it.

terms.meaning: The endoderm is the inner germ layer. It makes the inner lining of the gut, and the liver, the pancreas and the lining of the lungs.
terms.example: The thin lining of your stomach, which touches your food, came from the endoderm.
terms.art: The bottom sheet of a three-layer stack coloured yellow, with small drawings of a stomach, a liver and a pair of lungs beside it.

terms.meaning: The neural tube is a hollow tube of cells along the back of the embryo. It forms when a flat strip of ectoderm rolls up and its two edges join. It becomes the brain and the spinal cord.
terms.example: In a human embryo the neural tube has closed by about day 28.
terms.art: Three small cross-sections in a row: a flat sheet, the same sheet bent into a U, and a closed tube under a covering sheet.

terms.meaning: In an embryo, a signal is a chemical that some cells release and other cells sense. Cells that sense it change what they do.
terms.example: A signal protein called Sonic hedgehog is made at the little-finger edge of a growing hand.
terms.art: A small group of cells at one edge of a paddle-shaped hand bud, with dots spreading from them and getting fewer further away.

terms.meaning: A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for making one protein. This is a simplified meaning, because some genes make other useful molecules.
terms.example: You have about 20,000 genes that carry instructions for proteins.
terms.art: A long twisted DNA ladder with one short stretch of it shaded and labelled 'one gene'.

terms.meaning: A master switch gene makes a protein that turns many other genes on or off. So one master switch gene can start the building of a whole part.
terms.example: The gene called Pax6 is a master switch gene for building an eye.
terms.art: One large switch on a wall with wires running from it to many small lamps, some lit and some dark.

terms.meaning: Hox genes are a family of master switch genes. Different Hox genes are switched on at different places from the head end to the tail end, so they mark where each part of the body is.
terms.example: Humans have 39 Hox genes, and a fruit fly has 8.
terms.art: A row of coloured blocks on a line of DNA, with a line from each block to a matching coloured band on the body of a mouse embryo.

terms.meaning: A homeotic change is when one body part grows in the place of another because a master switch gene was changed. The part itself is well made. Only the place is wrong.
terms.example: A fruit fly with a homeotic change can have legs on their head where the antennae should be.
terms.art: The head of a fruit fly seen from the front, with two small legs growing where the two antennae normally are.

terms.meaning: Regeneration is growing back a lost body part, with the right tissues in the right places.
terms.example: An axolotl who loses a leg regenerates a new leg with bones, muscles, nerves and toes.
terms.art: A pink axolotl with feathery gills, one front leg shorter than the other and tipped with a small pale bud.

terms.meaning: A blastema is the bud of dividing cells that forms on the stump after an animal such as an axolotl loses a limb. The new limb grows from it.
terms.example: About a week or two after an axolotl loses a leg, a cone-shaped blastema can be seen on the stump.
terms.art: A close view of the stump of an axolotl's leg with a small smooth cone of pale cells at its tip.

terms.meaning: Positional memory means that a cell in a grown body still keeps a record of where in the body they are. The record is kept as certain genes that stay switched on.
terms.example: Because of positional memory, an axolotl cut at the wrist regrows only a hand, and not a whole arm.
terms.art: An axolotl's front leg drawn with a different colour band at the shoulder, elbow, wrist and toes, like addresses on a street.

explanations.concept: One cell divides into a ball of cells
explanations.definition: Cleavage is the first set of cell divisions. The fertilised egg cell divides into 2, 4, 8 and 16 smaller cells and becomes a solid ball called a morula.
explanations.description: A fertilised human egg cell is about a tenth of a millimetre across, about as wide as a hair is thick. It is one of the biggest cells in the body. About a day after fertilisation it divides into two cells. These divide again, roughly once a day at first. The embryo does not eat during these days, so they cannot grow. Each division just shares out what was in the egg cell, and the cells get smaller each time. By about day 4 there are around 16 cells in a solid ball, the morula. By about day 5 the ball has become hollow, with a small clump of cells inside. That clump will become the whole body. The outer cells will help make the placenta. Why divide first, before building anything? Because building needs many small cells that can move, fold and take different jobs. One giant cell cannot fold.
examples: Cut a ball of chapati dough into 2, then 4, then 8 pieces. You have more pieces, but no more dough. Cleavage is like that.
A frog's egg is big enough to see with your eyes. In a pond you can watch one cell become two in a few hours.
The 8 cells of a human embryo on day 3 fit inside the same thin coat that held the one egg cell.
explanations.art: The same-sized circle drawn five times in a row, holding 1 cell, 2 cells, 4 cells, a solid ball of 16 cells, and a hollow ball with a small clump of cells inside.

explanations.concept: Gastrulation: the embryo becomes three layers
explanations.definition: Gastrulation is the movement of cells in the early embryo that arranges them into three layers: an outer, a middle and an inner one.
explanations.description: In the second week the cells that will become the body lie in a flat, round disc, like a tiny dosa two layers thick. On about day 14 or 15 a groove appears along part of the top layer. It is called the primitive streak. Cells of the top layer crawl towards the groove, dive through it and spread out underneath. The first cells to dive in form the inner layer. Later ones settle between the top and the bottom and form the middle layer. The cells that stay on top are the outer layer. So after about a week of moving, the disc has three layers. The streak also shows the body's directions for the first time. The end where it starts is the tail end. The other end is the head end. Its line divides left from right. The scientist Lewis Wolpert said that the most important time in your life is not birth or marriage, but gastrulation. He meant that everything built later depends on these layers and directions.
examples: Before gastrulation, an embryo can still split and become identical twins. Once the streak has formed, there is one body plan, with one head end and one tail end.
In a sea urchin or a frog, gastrulation looks different. A hollow ball of cells pushes inwards at one spot, like a finger pressed into a soft ball. The result is the same: layers inside layers.
At the end of gastrulation a human embryo is about 2 millimetres long. Most mothers do not yet know that they are pregnant.
explanations.art: A flat oval disc seen from above with a groove running from one end to the middle, and beside it a cut-through view showing cells diving through the groove and forming a middle and a bottom layer.

explanations.concept: The three germ layers and what each one makes
explanations.definition: The three germ layers are the ectoderm (outer), the mesoderm (middle) and the endoderm (inner). Each one makes a particular set of tissues.
explanations.description: The ectoderm makes the body's outer covering and its nervous system: the outer layer of the skin, hair, nails, the hard enamel of teeth, the brain, the spinal cord and the nerves. The mesoderm makes what holds the body up and moves things about: muscles, bones, the heart, blood, blood vessels, the kidneys and the deeper layer of the skin. The endoderm makes the lining of the long tube that food passes through, from the throat to the far end. It also makes the organs that bud off that tube: the liver, the pancreas and the lining of the lungs. Most organs are made by more than one layer working together. In your stomach, the lining is endoderm, the muscle wall is mesoderm and the nerves are ectoderm. Why does it seem odd that brain and skin are the same layer? Because we sort body parts by what they do. The embryo sorts them by where their cells started.
examples: Your fingernail and your brain both come from the ectoderm. Your thigh bone and your blood both come from the mesoderm.
The lungs begin as a small bud that grows out of the food tube. That is why the windpipe and the food pipe meet in your throat.

A group of ectoderm cells called the neural crest leaves the back of the embryo and travels far. These cells make much of the face, the colour cells of the skin and the nerves of the gut. Some scientists call them a fourth layer.
explanations.art: An outline of a child's body with parts coloured in three colours: blue for skin, brain and nerves, red for bones, muscles and heart, yellow for the food tube, liver and lungs.

explanations.concept: Folding: how flat sheets become tubes
explanations.definition: A sheet of cells bends when the cells on one face of the sheet become narrower or wider than the cells on the other face. Folding turns the flat embryo into a body made of tubes.
explanations.description: After gastrulation the embryo is still flat. In the fourth week it folds. Along the back, a strip of ectoderm thickens. The cells along its middle line change shape. Each cell has a ring of protein threads near its top, made of the same two proteins that make muscles pull. The ring tightens like the drawstring of a cloth bag. The top of the cell becomes narrow while the bottom stays wide, so the cell becomes wedge-shaped. A row of wedges cannot lie flat. The sheet bends into a groove, the edges rise, meet and join, and a tube pinches off under the skin. This is the neural tube, the start of the brain and spinal cord. Pushing from the tissue on both sides helps the edges meet. At the same time the whole disc curls. Its sides fold down and meet along the belly, and the endoderm is rolled up inside as the gut tube. You are, roughly, a tube inside a tube. If the neural tube does not close fully, the baby is born with a gap in the spine or skull. Enough folate, a B vitamin found in green leaves and dals, lowers that risk. So doctors give folic acid tablets to women who may become pregnant.
examples: In the Curling Strip Test, strips of spring onion curl in water because the cells on one face swell more than the cells on the other face. The cause is different from the embryo's, but the geometry is the same.
A papad held over a flame curls for a similar reason. The heated face changes size before the other face does.
The neural tube closes like two zips, starting in the middle around day 22. The head end closes at about day 25 and the tail end by about day 28.
explanations.art: Four cross-sections in a row showing a flat sheet of tall cells, the middle cells turning wedge-shaped, the sheet bent into a deep groove, and a closed tube lying under a new flat covering sheet.

explanations.concept: Organs begin: the heart works while it is still being built
explanations.definition: Organs form from buds, folds and tubes of the germ layers, mostly between week 3 and week 8. The heart is the first organ to work.
explanations.description: A heart does not appear ready-made. Two thin tubes of mesoderm form on either side of the embryo. As the body folds, they are brought together in the middle and join into one tube. On about day 22 that tube starts to squeeze in a rhythm. It has no rooms and no valves yet, but it is already moving blood. Why so early? Until then, food and oxygen simply seep from cell to cell. Seeping works only over very short distances, and the embryo has grown too thick for it. Over the next weeks the beating tube grows longer than its space, so it bends into a loop. Walls grow inside and divide it into four chambers. It never stops beating while this happens. Other organs start as buds. The arms begin as two small bumps at about day 26, and the legs about two days later. The lungs begin as a bud from the food tube that branches again and again. By the end of week 8 the embryo is about 3 centimetres long, and every main organ has been started. From then until birth the baby is called a fetus, and the work is mostly growing and finishing.
examples: A cycle cannot be ridden until it is finished. An embryo's heart is used from the day it is a simple tube, and is rebuilt while in use.
Your arm began as a bump about the size of a pinhead on the side of an embryo 4 millimetres long.
A chick embryo's heart can be seen beating through a window cut in the eggshell after about two days of warming. This is how many of these facts were first found.
explanations.art: Four small drawings of a heart in a row: two side-by-side tubes, one straight tube, a tube bent into an S-shaped loop, and a four-chambered heart.

explanations.concept: How cells know where they are: signals from their neighbours
explanations.definition: Cells in an embryo release chemical signals, and other cells sense how much signal reaches them. From this a cell can tell where they are, and they switch on the genes that fit that place.
explanations.description: Nearly every cell in an embryo carries the same DNA. So a cell cannot find their job by reading something that only they have. They find it by sensing their surroundings. The hand is the best-studied example. A hand begins as a flat paddle. A small group of cells at the little-finger edge of the paddle makes a signal protein called Sonic hedgehog. The protein spreads across the paddle and thins out with distance. Cells that sense a lot of it, for a long time, build a little finger. Cells further away, which sense less, build the middle fingers. Cells that sense almost none build the thumb. In 1968 John Saunders and Mary Gasseling cut out those signalling cells from one chick embryo. They placed them on the thumb edge of another embryo's wing bud. That wing grew as a mirror image, with two sets of fingers back to back. In 1993 the team of Cliff Tabin found the signal itself. The fuller picture is that the amount is not the whole story. How long a cell is bathed in the signal, and which genes that cell already has switched on, matter too.
examples: Some babies are born with an extra finger or toe on the thumb side. In some families this comes from a small change in the DNA that makes Sonic hedgehog switch on at the thumb edge as well.
The same Sonic hedgehog signal is used again in the neural tube, where it tells cells whether they are near the belly side or the back side.
In the Mirror Wing activity you count how far each finger is from a coin, and see how a second coin makes a mirror hand.

perspectives.explanation: The signal locks onto a receptor, a chain of chemical steps follows, and certain genes switch on. On this view, 'the cell works out where they are' is only a short way of describing that chain of chemistry.

explanations.art: A paddle-shaped hand bud with a small patch of cells at the little-finger edge, dots spreading from the patch and thinning out, and faint outlines of five fingers with the little finger nearest the patch.

explanations.concept: Hox genes mark each place from head to tail
explanations.definition: Hox genes are master switch genes. Different Hox genes are on at different places along the body, from behind the head to the tail, and the set that is on tells the cells which part to build there.
explanations.description: Signals tell a cell roughly where they are. The cell then needs to keep that information, even after the signal has gone. Hox genes do this. Each Hox gene makes a protein that grips DNA at certain spots and turns other genes on or off. Near the head end only the first few Hox genes are on. Further back, more of them are on. So each stretch of the body has its own set, like an address. In your backbone the address decides the kind of bone. Seven neck bones have no ribs. Twelve chest bones each carry a pair of ribs. Five lower back bones have none. One odd fact shows how address-like these genes are. On the chromosome, the Hox genes sit in a row, and their order in the row is the same as the order of the body parts they mark, from head end to tail end. A Hox gene does not hold the instructions for a rib or a leg. Those are in hundreds of other genes. The Hox gene only says which of them to use here. The very front of the head is marked by other switch genes, not by Hox genes.
examples: A mouse normally has 13 chest bones with ribs, then 6 lower back bones without. In 2003 Deneen Wellik and Mario Capecchi switched off the mouse's Hox10 genes. The lower back bones then grew ribs, as if their address said 'chest'.
About 1 person in every 100 or 200 has a small extra rib on the lowest neck bone. Most never notice it.
A giraffe has seven neck bones, the same number as you and as a mouse. Each bone is just very long.
explanations.art: A side view of a mouse embryo with coloured bands along the back from neck to tail, and below it a row of coloured blocks on a strand of DNA in the same order as the bands.

explanations.concept: A changed Hox gene: the right part in the wrong place
explanations.definition: A homeotic change is a change in a master switch gene that makes one body part grow where another should be.
explanations.description: Fruit flies showed what Hox genes do. A fly's body is a row of segments. The middle part has three segments. The second carries the wings. The third carries two tiny knobs called halteres, which help the fly balance. Edward Lewis in California studied one Hox gene, Ultrabithorax, for more than thirty years. It is on in the third segment. When it is switched off there, the third segment builds what the second segment builds. The fly has four wings. In another fly, a Hox gene called Antennapedia is switched on in the head, where it should be off. The cells there read the address 'middle of the body' and build legs where the antennae should be. In both flies every part is properly made. A leg on the head has all its joints and bristles. This tells us something about how bodies are built. The instructions for a part work as one package. A master switch only has to say where to run the package.
examples: A fly with four wings has not gained a new gene for wings. They have lost the switch that said 'not here'.
In the Address Game, a 'changed switch' card makes your creature build a good part in the wrong place.
The English scientist William Bateson collected hundreds of such cases in animals and plants, and in 1894 he gave them the name 'homeosis'.
explanations.art: Two fruit flies side by side seen from above: an ordinary fly with two wings and two tiny knobs behind them, and a fly with four full wings.

explanations.concept: The same switch genes build a fly and you
explanations.definition: Nearly all animals with a head end and a tail end use the same family of Hox genes to mark places along the body. The genes were inherited from an ancestor they all share.
explanations.description: A fly and a human look as different as two animals can. Until the 1980s most biologists were sure their bodies were built by quite different genes. Then, in 1984, two teams found that the fly's Hox genes all share one short stretch of DNA, 180 letters long. They named it the homeobox. When they searched other animals for the same stretch, they found it in beetles, worms, frogs, mice and humans. A fly has 8 Hox genes in one row. A human has 39, in four rows on four chromosomes. The four rows came about because the whole set was copied twice in our fish-like ancestors, long ago, and some copies were lost later. The order within each row still matches the order along the body. So the last ancestor that flies and humans share, probably a small worm-like animal that lived more than 500 million years ago, already marked their body from head to tail with these genes. The parts have changed beyond recognition. The way of marking where they go has been kept.
examples: A mouse Hox gene put into a fly embryo can do some of the work of the fly's own matching Hox gene.
A centipede, a prawn and a snake all use Hox genes to tell the front of the body from the back.
A jellyfish, who has no head end or tail end of this kind, has only a few Hox-like genes.
explanations.art: A fruit fly above and a human embryo below, each with coloured bands along the body, and between them two rows of coloured blocks in the same colour order.

explanations.concept: Pax6: one switch that says 'build an eye here'
explanations.definition: Pax6 is a master switch gene that starts the building of an eye. The same gene does this job in flies, mice, squid and humans.
explanations.description: Flies with a broken copy of this gene have no eyes, so fly scientists named it 'eyeless'. In 1995 Georg Halder, Patrick Callaerts and Walter Gehring in Basel, Switzerland, did the opposite test. They switched the gene on in parts of a young fly where it is normally off. The flies grew extra eyes on their wings, legs and antennae. These were real fly eyes, with the full set of light-catching cells. Then the team used the matching gene from a mouse. The fly again grew extra eyes. They were fly eyes, not mouse eyes. This is the clearest test of what a master switch is. The mouse gene did not carry a plan for a mouse eye. It only said 'build an eye here', and the fly's cells built the kind of eye that flies build. The fuller picture is that Pax6 does not work alone. A handful of switch genes turn each other on, and the eye is built only when the whole group is running.
examples: People who inherit one broken copy of PAX6 are usually born with no iris, the coloured ring of the eye.
A switch on a wall does not hold the light. The same switch could run a fan in another house.
A fly's eye has hundreds of tiny lenses and a mouse's eye has one. The same switch gene starts both.
explanations.art: A fruit fly seen from the side with one small red eye growing on a leg and another on a wing, as well as the normal eyes on the head.

explanations.concept: Patterns that nobody draws: how five fingers may be spaced
explanations.description: Signals that fade with distance can mark one edge from the other. But what makes a repeated pattern, such as finger, gap, finger, gap? In 1952 the English mathematician Alan Turing suggested an answer, using only pencil-and-paper maths. Imagine two chemicals that cells make. The first one makes cells produce more of both. The second one spreads faster and stops the first. Start with an even mix, and tiny chance differences grow. Peaks of the first chemical appear, each surrounded by a zone where the second chemical blocks any other peak. The peaks end up evenly spaced, as spots or as stripes. For decades nobody could find such chemicals in an animal. In 2014 the team of James Sharpe in Barcelona showed that three known signals in a mouse's growing paw behave this way, and their computer model drew stripes where the fingers form. This is now the leading idea for how fingers are spaced. It is not proved for humans, and other scientists think the pulling and squeezing of the cells themselves plays a part as well.
examples: When Sharpe's team weakened one of the signals in mouse paws, the fingers came out with different spacing, as the model predicted.
The stripes of a zebrafish and the spots of a leopard may form in a related way, though the details differ.
Ripples of sand on a beach are evenly spaced too, and nobody places them. Their cause is different, but they also show a pattern with no drawing behind it.
explanations.art: A paddle-shaped paw bud with five evenly spaced dark stripes fanning out from the wrist, and beside it a small square showing evenly spaced spots.

explanations.concept: Regrowing: how an axolotl replaces a lost leg
explanations.definition: Regeneration is growing back a lost part with the right tissues in the right places. An axolotl can regenerate legs, the tail, and parts of the spinal cord, heart and brain.
explanations.description: The axolotl is a salamander from the lakes and canals of Xochimilco, in Mexico City. She keeps her feathery gills and lives under water all her life. If she loses a leg, skin cells crawl over the wound within about a day. Under this cover, cells near the cut stop doing their grown-up jobs and start dividing. They form a bud called a blastema. Over some weeks the blastema grows and shapes itself into the missing part, with bones, muscles, nerves and toes. Two findings explain why the new leg comes out right. In 2009 Martin Kragl, Elly Tanaka and their team gave the cells of each tissue a glowing mark and followed them. Muscle cells made new muscle. Cartilage cells did not make muscle. So the cells do not become blank. They remember what tissue they were. In 2025 Leo Otsuki, Tanaka and their team found a memory of place as well. Cells on the little-finger side of the leg keep a gene called Hand2 switched on for life. After a cut, those cells switch Sonic hedgehog on again, the same signal that shaped the leg in the embryo. So regrowing is the embryo's method, run again by cells that kept their addresses.
examples: An axolotl cut at the wrist regrows a hand. Cut at the shoulder, she regrows the whole arm. The blastema builds only what is missing.
A house gecko who drops their tail grows a new one. But the new tail has a plain rod of cartilage inside, where the first tail had a row of small bones.
Wild axolotls are close to dying out, because their lakes have been drained and polluted. Many thousands live in laboratories and aquariums.
explanations.art: Four small drawings of an axolotl's front leg in a row: just cut at the elbow, covered with skin, tipped with a cone-shaped bud, and regrown with four small toes.

explanations.concept: Vitamin A and the legs that grew from a tail
explanations.definition: Retinoic acid, a chemical the body makes from vitamin A, is one of the signals that tells the cells of a limb how far they are from the shoulder. Too much of it resets their address.
explanations.description: In the 1970s, at the University of Rajasthan in Jaipur, Professor I. A. Niazi and his student Saroj Saxena cut the back legs of toad tadpoles and added extra vitamin A to their water. They wanted to see what the vitamin would do. In many tadpoles the stump grew far more than was missing, sometimes whole extra legs. Their papers of 1977 and 1978 were the first reports of this. In 1982 Malcolm Maden in London tested it carefully in axolotls. A leg cut at the wrist normally regrows a hand. With retinoic acid, the wrist stump grew a whole new arm, from shoulder to fingers, stuck onto the old one. The chemical had changed the cells' address from 'wrist' to 'shoulder', and they built everything from the shoulder outwards. In 1992 Priyambada Mohanty-Hejmadi and her team at Utkal University in Bhubaneswar went a step further. They cut the tails of tadpoles of the marbled balloon frog and gave them vitamin A. Some tadpoles grew legs where the tail had been. A tail address had been changed into a hip address.
examples: A tadpole with legs growing from the tail stump has no new genes. One chemical changed which address the cells read.
This is why very high doses of vitamin A medicines are dangerous in pregnancy. They can upset the addresses in an embryo.
The right amount of vitamin A, from foods such as carrot, papaya, drumstick leaves and milk, is needed for healthy eyes and for an embryo's normal growth.
explanations.art: A frog tadpole seen from above with a cluster of small extra back legs growing from the stump where the tail was cut.

explanations.concept: Why can an axolotl regrow a leg when a human cannot?
explanations.description: Humans do regenerate some things. The outer skin, the lining of the gut and the blood are replaced all the time. A liver with a part cut away grows back to its full weight in weeks. A young child who loses the very tip of a finger can often grow it back if the base of the nail is still there. The English doctor Cynthia Illingworth reported this in 1974. In mice, Mayumi Ito's team showed in 2013 that the cells at the base of the nail send the signals that make the fingertip regrow. But a human who loses a hand heals with a scar. Scientists do not agree on why.
examples: Deer are mammals, and a stag regrows a full set of antlers, bone and all, every year.
A zebrafish, a small striped fish first found in the rivers of Bengal and Bihar, can regrow fins and even part of the heart.
In the Nail Clock experiment you measure how fast one part of you is still being built.

perspectives.explanation: Mammals close wounds fast with a scar. A scar stops bleeding and infection quickly, which matters for a warm-blooded animal on land. But scar tissue blocks the signals a blastema needs.

Regrowing needs grown cells to start dividing freely again. In a long-lived animal, cells that divide freely can turn into cancers. Our bodies may keep such cells under tight control, at the cost of regrowing.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study axolotls, such as Elly Tanaka and Jessica Whited
perspectives.explanation: Humans have nearly all the genes that an axolotl uses, and a child's fingertip shows the method still works in us. The ability may be switched off rather than lost, and might be switched on again one day.

explanations.art: A child's hand with a small plaster on one fingertip next to an axolotl's hand with a regrowing bud, and a question mark between them.

explanations.concept: Is the plan of the body written in the DNA?
explanations.description: People often call DNA the blueprint of the body. A blueprint is a drawing in which each part of the drawing matches one part of the building. DNA is not like that. No stretch of DNA is a picture of a hand. DNA lists proteins and the conditions for making them. The shape appears as cells make those proteins, signal to their neighbours, move, pull and fold. So where is the shape stored? Scientists give different answers.
examples: A recipe for dosa batter does not contain a picture of a dosa. The round shape comes from pouring and spreading.
In the Rule, Not the Drawing challenge you write rules for single coins, and a body pattern appears that no rule mentions.
Flatworms that were made to grow two heads kept growing two heads after being cut again, though their DNA had not been changed.

perspectives.explanation: Everything needed is in the fertilised egg cell: the DNA, and the molecules the mother packed into the egg. The shape is not drawn anywhere, but it follows from them step by step, as a cake follows from a recipe and an oven.

perspectives.who: Michael Levin and his team at Tufts University
perspectives.explanation: Groups of cells also store a pattern in the electrical charges they hold and share, a little as a brain stores a memory. Changing that pattern can change the body's shape with no change in the DNA. Many biologists are not yet convinced this works in most animals.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study the forces in tissues
perspectives.explanation: Much of the shape comes from plain mechanics. Sheets buckle, tubes loop and buds branch because of how they are squeezed and stretched. Genes set the conditions, and physics does the shaping.

explanations.art: A strand of DNA on the left, a simple recipe card in the middle and a drawn plan of a house on the right, with a tick over the recipe card and a question mark over the house plan.

explanations.definition: The signals and switch genes that build an embryo keep working in a grown body, where they replace worn-out cells, heal wounds and keep each part the right size.
explanations.description: Being born is not the end of being built. Your skeleton is being taken apart and rebuilt a little every day. The outer layer of your skin is replaced about once a month. Your nails and hair grow from groups of dividing cells that never stop. When you cut your knee, cells at the edge of the wound crawl over it in a sheet, much as cells crawl during gastrulation. The same signals are used. This has a dangerous side. Many cancers start when one of the embryo's building signals, such as Sonic hedgehog, gets stuck in the 'on' position in a grown body. Cells then keep dividing as if they were still building. So some new cancer medicines work by blocking those signals. A body is something its cells keep doing for as long as it lives.
examples: A fingernail grows about three and a half millimetres in a month. In the Nail Clock experiment you measure your own.
A broken arm bone knits itself together in about six weeks in a child. The cells first lay down soft cartilage and then turn it to bone, as they did before birth.
The lining of your small intestine is replaced about every five days.
explanations.art: A child's hand with a small dot of nail polish halfway up one nail, and a dotted outline near the base of the nail showing where the dot was three weeks earlier.

agreed.text: Every human body begins as one cell, and every part is built afterwards. No tiny ready-made body lies hidden in the egg cell.
agreed.evidence: Embryos of chicks, frogs, mice and humans have been watched and photographed at every stage. The parts appear one after another, from cells that at first look alike.
agreed.context: This card says what scientists agree on about how a body begins.

agreed.text: Early in growth, the cells of an animal embryo arrange themselves into layers, and each layer makes a particular set of tissues.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have marked single cells in early embryos with dyes and glowing proteins, and followed where their daughter cells end up.
agreed.context: This card says what scientists agree on about the germ layers of an embryo.

agreed.text: Flat sheets of cells fold into tubes because the cells themselves change shape and move.
agreed.evidence: Under the microscope, cells along the folding line of the neural tube can be seen narrowing at one end. Blocking the protein threads that tighten them stops the folding.
agreed.context: This card says what scientists agree on about how an embryo folds.

agreed.text: Cells in an embryo find out where they are from chemical signals made by other cells.
agreed.evidence: Moving the signalling cells of a chick's wing bud to the other edge gives a mirror-image wing (Saunders and Gasseling, 1968). The signal was later found to be the protein Sonic hedgehog (1993).
agreed.context: This card says what scientists agree on about how cells in an embryo know their place.

agreed.text: Hox genes mark places along the body from head end to tail end, and animals as different as flies, mice and humans use the same family of genes for this.
agreed.evidence: Changing one Hox gene makes a normal part grow in the wrong place, in flies and in mice. The same 180-letter stretch of DNA is found in the Hox genes of all these animals.
agreed.context: This card says what scientists agree on about Hox genes.

agreed.text: When an axolotl regrows a leg, the cells of the stump keep a memory of what tissue they were and where they were.
agreed.evidence: Cells marked with a glowing protein were followed through regrowth (Kragl and others, 2009). Cells on one side of the leg keep the gene Hand2 on for life (Otsuki and others, 2025).
agreed.context: This card says what scientists agree on about how an axolotl regrows a leg.

challenging.claim: DNA is the blueprint of the body.
challenging.who: Many school books and news reports
challenging.for: A change in the DNA can change the body, and identical twins, who share their DNA, look alike. So the information for building a body is passed on in the DNA.
challenging.against: A blueprint is a drawing where each part matches a part of the building. No stretch of DNA matches a hand. DNA lists proteins and when to make them. The same mouse gene Pax6 gives a fly eye in a fly. A recipe, or a set of rules, is a closer comparison.
challenging.context: This card is about a common saying: that DNA is the blueprint of the body.

challenging.claim: Each gene builds one part of the body.
challenging.for: Some genes are named after one part, such as 'eyeless'. Losing one gene can remove one part.
challenging.against: The signal Sonic hedgehog helps shape the hand, the spinal cord, the face, the teeth and the hair. Most genes are used in many places and at many times. A gene's name usually records only the first thing scientists saw go wrong.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that each gene builds one body part.

challenging.claim: Humans have lost the ability to regenerate.
challenging.for: A human who loses an arm or a leg heals with a scar and never regrows it.
challenging.against: Young children can regrow a lost fingertip if the base of the nail remains. The liver regrows to its full weight. Humans carry nearly all the genes that an axolotl uses. The ability may be held back, not gone.
challenging.context: This card is about the claim that humans cannot regenerate body parts.

challenging.claim: The body's shape is remembered partly in electrical signals between cells, and not only in genes.
challenging.who: Michael Levin and his team at Tufts University, United States
challenging.for: The team briefly blocked the tiny channels that join the cells of cut flatworms. Some worms grew two heads. Cut again weeks later, in plain water, they grew two heads again. Their DNA had not been changed.
challenging.against: The work has been done mostly in flatworms and frog tadpoles. Many biologists think the electrical changes are one more signal that switches genes, and not a separate store of the body's shape.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that cells store the body's shape in electrical signals as well as in genes.

challenging.claim: A snake has a long body with no legs because the Hox genes for 'chest' are switched on along almost the whole body.
challenging.who: Martin Cohn and Cheryll Tickle, in a study of python embryos, 1999
challenging.for: In python embryos, Hox genes that mark the chest in other animals are on nearly all the way from the head to the hips. Nearly every bone of a python's back carries ribs.
challenging.against: Later studies found that snakes still have small differences between regions of the backbone, and that their Hox genes are on in the usual order. Changes in how the body's cells answer the Hox genes seem to matter too.
challenging.context: This card is about one explanation of why a snake's body is long and legless.

big_questions.q: If no cell holds a picture of the whole body, where is the shape of your body kept?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Rule, Not the Drawing. Where was the coin pattern before the rules were followed?

big_questions.q: The same Pax6 gene builds a fly's eye in a fly and a mouse's eye in a mouse. So what does a gene 'mean' by itself?
big_questions.hint: Think about a word that means different things in two languages.

big_questions.q: An axolotl's cells remember where they are for her whole life. In what ways does your body remember things that your mind does not?
big_questions.hint: Think about a scar, a vaccination, and the cells in the Nail Clock.

big_questions.q: Your heart was working while it was still being built. Is there any time when you were finished? Will there be?
big_questions.hint: Think about your nails, your skin and your bones, which are still being rebuilt.

big_questions.q: A fly and you use the same genes to mark head from tail. What does that say about how closely you and a fly are related?
big_questions.hint: Think about two families who use the same unusual recipe. Where might they have got it?

big_questions.q: If doctors could switch on regrowing in humans, should they? What could go wrong, and who should decide?
big_questions.hint: Think about why cells that divide freely can be dangerous, and about who could pay for such a treatment.

story.title: The Braid Nobody Knew
story.note: A made-up story. Kayal, Muthu, Ponni akka and Selvi teacher are imagined. Pinnal kolattam is real. It is a dance from Tamil Nadu in which dancers hold ropes that hang from a pole, and weave the ropes into a braid by the way they move past each other. One wrong move can spoil the braid. The two rules in the story are a simple way such braids can be made. Real troupes use many different steps, and the patterns described here are imagined.
text: Eight ropes hung from an iron ring at the top of the pole in the school yard. Four were red and four were white. For three weeks, eight girls had danced round that pole every evening, and every evening a braid had grown down it, red and white in neat checks, like the skin of a snake.

Ponni akka made it happen. She was sixteen, and she called out every beat in a voice that carried to the tank. Kayal, who was ten and held the third white rope, did what the voice said and tried not to think.
Three days before the festival, Ponni akka woke up with a fever and spots.
"Then there is no dance," said one of the older girls that evening. "Only Ponni knows the braid."
Nobody argued. Selvi teacher, who had taught them, was away in Thanjavur for her daughter's wedding. The eight ropes hung straight and still.

Kayal went home and tried to draw the braid. She drew the pole, and eight lines going round it, over and under. By the fourth crossing her page looked like a plate of idiyappam. She tore it out and tried again. It was worse.
In the morning she walked to Ponni akka's house and stood at the window, because nobody was allowed inside.
"Akka, tell me the whole braid. I will write it down. Every crossing."
Ponni akka laughed, and the laugh turned into a cough. "I don't know the whole braid."
"You do. You call it."

"I call the beat, kanna. Listen. Reds walk towards the tank. Whites walk towards the road. When someone comes at you, pass her on the inside. Pass the next one on the outside. Then inside again. That is all Selvi teacher ever told me. That is all there is."
"But the checks. The pattern."
"I have never once thought about the pattern," said Ponni akka. "I am busy not bumping into people."

Kayal walked back slowly. A rope's colour told a dancer which way to go. The girl coming towards her told her which side to pass. Nobody needed the page that looked like idiyappam. Nobody had ever had it.
That evening there were only seven girls, so Kayal brought her brother Muthu, who was seven and had only ever watched. She put the fourth red rope in his hand.
"I don't know the dance," he said.
"Nobody does. You are red, so you walk towards the tank. Pass the first person on the inside and the next on the outside. Keep doing that. Don't look at the pole."

She clapped the beat herself. Her voice did not carry to the tank, but it carried round the pole. Reds one way, whites the other, in and out. For a minute it was only people trying not to bump into each other. Then one of the girls looked up and gasped. A braid was coming down the pole in neat red and white checks.
At the height of Kayal's shoulder, it went wrong. A lump appeared, two reds lying side by side where a red and a white should cross.
Everybody stopped. Nobody had seen who did it. But the braid had kept the mistake, at the exact place where it happened, for all of them to see.
"I think I passed two people on the same side," said Muthu, in a very small voice.
One of the older girls took hold of the lump and pulled. It only tightened.
"Wait," said Kayal. "We made it by walking. We can unmake it by walking." She turned to face the other way. "Everyone go back the way you came. Outside where you went inside. Slowly."

They walked backwards through their own steps. The braid opened from the bottom, crossing by crossing, until the lump loosened and fell apart into two plain ropes. Above it the checks were as neat as before.
"Now forwards," said Kayal.

On the night of the festival, one of the white ropes had no dancer, because her family's bus was late. Seven dancers took their places round the pole under the lamps. Kayal's stomach hurt. She had no time to work out what seven would do.

She did not need to. Reds towards the tank, whites towards the road, inside, outside. The braid that came down the pole was not the braid of checks. The colours ran in slanting bands, a pattern none of them had seen before, and it was even all the way down.
Afterwards Muthu stood looking up at it with his rope still in his hand.
"Who made that one?" he asked. "Which of us?"
Kayal opened her mouth to answer. She looked at the seven dancers, and at the pole, and at the braid that none of them had ever seen until it was there.
"Hold your rope," she said at last. "We have to walk it back."
story.epiphany: Kayal thought someone had to know the whole braid. Nobody did. Each dancer knew only two small things: her rope's colour told her which way to walk, and the person coming towards her told her which side to pass. The braid appeared when everyone followed those rules. Cells build a body in a similar way. No cell holds a picture of a hand or a heart. Each cell senses where they are and what their neighbours are doing, and acts on that. The braid also kept Muthu's mistake at the exact place where he made it, as a body keeps a changed part at the place where a switch was wrong. And when one dancer was missing, the same rules still made a whole braid, as an embryo with fewer cells still makes a whole body.
ask: Why could Kayal not draw the braid, even though she had danced it for three weeks?
Ponni akka said she had never thought about the pattern. So where was the pattern before the dance began?
The lump showed where the mistake was made, but not who made it. What in an embryo is like that lump?
With seven dancers the same rules made a different braid, and it was still even. What does that tell you about rules compared with drawings?
Muthu asked which of them made the braid. What would you have answered?

A girl of ten sitting on a doorstep with a notebook page covered in a tangle of crossing lines, and a torn-out page beside her.
A girl standing outside a barred window, talking to an older girl who lies on a mat inside with spots on her face.

A close view of the braid on the pole with one lump where two red ropes lie side by side, and children looking up at it.
Seven dancers under festival lamps at night, and on the pole a braid with slanting bands of red and white.

games.title: The Address Game: build a creature with Hox switches
games.context: This is a dice-and-drawing game about Hox genes. Each number on the die is an address along the body, from 1 at the head end to 6 at the tail end. You build a creature one address at a time, and sometimes a changed switch puts a part in the wrong place.

printables.title: 4 animal rule cards to cut out
items: MOUSE. Address 1: the back of the head. Address 2: neck bones with no ribs. Address 3: chest bones with ribs, and front legs. Address 4: lower back bones with no ribs. Address 5: hip bones, and back legs. Address 6: tail bones.

FRUIT FLY. Address 1: a head with two antennae. Address 2: a segment with one pair of legs. Address 3: a segment with legs and a pair of wings. Address 4: a segment with legs and two tiny balance knobs. Address 5: belly segments with no legs. Address 6: the tail end.

PYTHON. Address 1: the back of the head. Address 2: a short neck. Address 3: back bones with ribs. Address 4: more back bones with ribs. Address 5: more back bones with ribs, and two tiny spurs where back legs would be. Address 6: tail bones.

CENTIPEDE. Address 1: a head with two antennae. Address 2: a segment with a pair of poison claws. Address 3: a segment with a pair of legs. Address 4: another segment with legs. Address 5: another segment with legs. Address 6: a last segment with two long back legs.

printables.title: 6 changed switch cards to cut out (the real case is on the back)

items.f: CHANGED SWITCH. Switch 4 is off. Address 4 builds whatever address 3 builds.
items.b: Real cases: a fruit fly with the Hox gene Ultrabithorax off in the third middle segment grows four wings. A mouse with the Hox10 genes off grows ribs on the lower back.

items.f: CHANGED SWITCH. Switch 3 is on at address 1 as well. Address 1 builds whatever address 3 builds.
items.b: Real case: a fruit fly with the Hox gene Antennapedia switched on in the head grows legs where the antennae should be. In the real fly only the legs appear, not the wings.

items.f: CHANGED SWITCH. Switch 5 is off. Address 5 builds whatever address 4 builds.
items.b: Real case: a mouse with the Hox11 genes off has no hip bones in the backbone. Those bones look like lower back bones instead.

items.f: CHANGED SWITCH. Switch 3 is on a little too far forward. Address 2 builds whatever address 3 builds.
items.b: Real case: about 1 person in every 100 or 200 has a small rib on the lowest neck bone. Most never notice it.

items.f: NO CHANGE. All your switches are working. Take one extra roll.
items.b: Most of the time, in most embryos, every Hox switch comes on in the right place.

items.f: NO CHANGE. All your switches are working. Take one extra roll.
items.b: A Hox switch does not hold the plan for a part. It says which part to build at this address.

printables.title: A creature sheet for each player (or draw six boxes in a row by hand)
items: Creature sheet. Head end: box 1, box 2, box 3, box 4, box 5, box 6: tail end. My animal: ____. Rolls I needed: ____.
Creature sheet. Head end: box 1, box 2, box 3, box 4, box 5, box 6: tail end. My animal: ____. Rolls I needed: ____.
Creature sheet. Head end: box 1, box 2, box 3, box 4, box 5, box 6: tail end. My animal: ____. Rolls I needed: ____.
Creature sheet. Head end: box 1, box 2, box 3, box 4, box 5, box 6: tail end. My animal: ____. Rolls I needed: ____.

rules: You need one die and a pencil for each player. Each player picks an animal rule card and a creature sheet with six boxes, numbered 1 at the head end to 6 at the tail end.
Shuffle the six changed switch cards and put them in a pile, face down.

On your turn, roll the die. The number is the address where a Hox switch has just come on. Draw the part your rule card gives for that address in that box. If the box is already drawn, pass the die on.
If you roll the same number as the player before you, take the top changed switch card. Keep it by your sheet and obey it for the rest of the game, redrawing a box if you need to.
The first player with all six boxes drawn wins. Each player then says how any changed part would help or trouble their animal.
Playing alone: take a changed switch card when you roll the same number twice running. Count your rolls, then play again with another animal and try to finish in fewer.

setup.art: A table with one die, four animal rule cards, a small face-down pile of cards and two paper sheets that each have six empty boxes in a row.
setup.caption: 1. Each player takes a rule card and a sheet with six boxes.

setup.art: A child's hand rolling a die that shows 3, and a pencil drawing ribs and front legs in box 3 of a creature sheet next to a card headed MOUSE.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die. Draw the part for that address.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the rule cards and the changed switch cards. 2. Each player picks an animal and draws six boxes in a row, or takes a creature sheet. 3. Read the rules together.
flow.say: Each box is one address along the body. Box 1 is at the head end and box 6 is at the tail end. The die tells us which Hox switch has come on.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Pick an animal. Draw six boxes in a row. Number them 1 to 6.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Address Game. Here you set up the cards and the creature sheets.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll and draw. 2. When a changed switch card comes up, read the front, obey it, then turn it over and read the real case. 3. Play until one creature is complete. 4. Play a second round with different animals if there is time.
flow.say: The same roll of 3 gives ribs in the mouse and wings in the fly. Does the switch hold the part, or only the address?
flow.kid: Roll the die. Draw the part for that address. Obey any changed switch card. Fill all six boxes.

ask.q: A changed switch card made address 4 build what address 3 builds. Was the new part badly made?
good: No, it was a normal part.
It was a good part in the wrong place.

flow.parent: Filling six boxes takes about 15 rolls for one player. Real animals have more than six Hox genes, and several are on at once in most places. The game keeps one switch for each address to stay simple.
flow.context: This is the main part of the Address Game. Here you roll the die and build your creature address by address.

flow.do: 1. Lay the finished creatures side by side. 2. Ask what the changed parts have in common. 3. Ask why the same card gave four wings in the fly and extra ribs in the mouse.
flow.say: Look at the creatures with a changed switch. What is the same about all the changes? Why did one card do different things to the fly and the mouse?
flow.kid: Put the creatures side by side. What is the same about every changed part?

check.q: A fruit fly with one Hox gene switched off grows four wings. What does that show about the Hox gene?
options: It carries the full plan for a wing
It tells a segment which part to build
It makes all body parts bigger
check.why: The extra wings are normal wings in the wrong segment. So the Hox gene did not hold the wing plan. It told the third segment 'you are not the wing segment'. Without it, the segment built what the segment in front builds.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Address Game. Here you compare the finished creatures and say what a Hox switch does.

games.title: Regrow, Half Regrow or Scar?
games.context: This is a card game about which animals can regrow which parts. Each card names an animal and a lost part. You hold up one, two or three fingers to say what happens next, then turn the card to check.

printables.title: 18 cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: An axolotl loses a front leg.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. A full leg grows back, with bones, muscles, nerves and toes.

items.f: A house gecko drops their tail to escape a cat.
items.b: 2. HALF REGROWS. A new tail grows, but it has a plain rod of cartilage inside in place of the small bones.

items.f: A grown-up human loses a hand.
items.b: 3. SCAR. The wound closes with a scar, and no new hand grows.

items.f: A four-year-old child loses the very tip of a finger. The base of the nail is still there.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. With simple care, the tip often grows back in a few weeks. The doctor Cynthia Illingworth reported this in 1974.

items.f: A chital stag sheds both antlers.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. A stag grows a full new pair of antlers, made of bone, every year.

items.f: A starfish loses one arm.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. A new arm grows from the stump over some months.

items.f: A flatworm from a pond is cut in two.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. Each piece grows the missing half and becomes a whole worm.

items.f: A surgeon removes half of a person's liver.
items.b: 2. HALF REGROWS. The part that is left grows back to the full weight in weeks, but not to the old shape.

items.f: A zebrafish loses the end of a fin.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. The fin grows back with its bony rays, usually within a few weeks.

items.f: A grown-up human loses a tooth from the second set.
items.b: 3. SCAR. The gum heals over. Humans grow only two sets of teeth.

items.f: A shark loses a tooth.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. Sharks grow new teeth all their lives, row behind row.

items.f: A crab loses a claw.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. A new claw appears at the next moults, small at first.

items.f: You graze the top layer of skin off your knee.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. Skin cells crawl over the graze and rebuild the top layer, usually with no mark.

items.f: A person has a deep cut that goes right through the skin.
items.b: 3. SCAR. The gap is filled with tough scar tissue, which has no hairs or sweat glands.

items.f: Part of a person's heart muscle dies in a heart attack.
items.b: 3. SCAR. The human heart replaces very few muscle cells. The damaged part becomes scar.

items.f: A zebrafish loses a piece of the heart.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. In about two months the missing heart muscle is replaced.

items.f: A hydra, a tiny pond animal, is cut into three pieces.
items.b: 1. REGROWS. Each piece becomes a whole small hydra.

items.f: A grown frog loses a back leg.
items.b: 3. SCAR. Grown frogs do not regrow legs. In the clawed frog, only a plain spike of cartilage grows.

rules: Shuffle the 18 cards and put them in a pile, question side up.
One player reads the top card aloud.

On the count of three, every player holds up fingers. One finger means REGROWS. Two fingers mean HALF REGROWS: something grows back, but it is not the same. Three fingers mean SCAR: nothing grows back.
Turn the card over and read the answer. Every player who was right scores one point.
After 18 cards, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: say your answer aloud before you turn each card. Try to reach 12 out of 18, then play again another day.

setup.art: A pile of small cards on a floor mat, with the top card showing a line of text, and two children sitting on either side.
setup.caption: 1. Put the 18 cards in a pile, question side up.

setup.art: Two children each holding up a hand, one showing one finger and the other showing three fingers, with a card held between them.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. On three, hold up one, two or three fingers.

setup.art: A card turned over on the mat showing its answer side, and a child making a tally mark on a slip of paper.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card to check. Score a point if you were right.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 18 cards. 2. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, question side up. 3. Practise the three hand signs.
flow.say: Each card names an animal who has lost a part. We guess what happens next: it regrows, it half regrows, or it heals with a scar.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Practise the signs: one finger, two fingers, three fingers.
flow.context: This is the first step of Regrow, Half Regrow or Scar? Here you set up the cards and learn the three hand signs.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Count to three. 3. Everyone holds up fingers. 4. Turn the card and read the answer. 5. Keep score.
flow.say: Think about what the animal would need to rebuild. Then show your answer on three.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. On three, hold up your fingers. Turn the card to check.

ask.q: Which answer surprised you most, and why?
good: That a child's fingertip can grow back.
That a gecko's new tail is not the same inside.
That a fish can regrow part of the heart and we cannot.

flow.parent: These answers are what usually happens. Real animals vary, and the answer for the child's fingertip depends on the nail base being left in place.
flow.context: This is the main part of Regrow, Half Regrow or Scar? Here you read each card and guess what happens to the lost part.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Sort the cards into three heaps by their answers. 3. Ask what your child notices about which animals are in the REGROWS heap.
flow.say: Look at the three heaps. Humans are in all three. What does that tell you about the saying that humans cannot regenerate?
flow.kid: Count your points. Sort the cards into three heaps. Which heaps have a human card?

check.q: A gecko's regrown tail has a rod of cartilage where the first tail had small bones. What does that show?
options: Regrowing is always perfect
Growing a part back is not always rebuilding it the same
Geckos cannot regrow anything
check.why: The gecko does grow a working tail, but the inside of the new tail is simpler than before. An axolotl rebuilds the same leg, bone for bone. So animals differ in how fully their cells can run the building steps again.

flow.context: This is the last step of Regrow, Half Regrow or Scar? Here you sort the cards and look for a pattern.

experiments.title: The Curling Strip Test: can a flat strip of cells bend itself?
experiments.context: An embryo starts flat and folds into tubes, with nothing outside doing the folding. In this experiment you find out how a flat sheet of living cells can bend with nobody bending it. You put flat strips of spring onion leaf into plain water, salt water and no water, and measure how much they curl.
experiments.question: Will a flat strip of spring onion leaf bend by itself in plain water, in salt water, or with no water? Which face of the strip ends up on the inside of the bend?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which strips will bend the most: the ones in plain water, the ones in salt water, or the dry ones? Which face will be on the inside of the bend, the shiny outer skin or the pale inner face? Write both guesses and your reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Change only what the strips lie in. Cut all nine strips from the same leaves, each 10 centimetres long and about as wide as a matchstick. Use cold water from the same jug for both tumblers. Leave all the strips for the same 20 minutes. Use three strips in each place, because one strip can be a fluke.
results_table: Gap between the two ends at the start (cm)
Which face is inside the bend

materials.item: spring onions with long, firm green leaves (the hollow green part is what you need)
steel tumblers or small bowls
a steel plate
cold drinking water, with a few ice cubes if you have them
table salt
a knife or kitchen scissors, used by a grown-up
a ruler, a spoon, a clock, a pencil and a notebook

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with the knife or scissors.

schedule.what: Cut nine strips of spring onion leaf. Put three in plain water, three in salt water and three on a dry plate. Measure the curl after 10 and 20 minutes, then swap the strips over.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with the mean gap for each place. Draw one strip from each place, and colour the shiny face green. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: mean gap between the two ends of a 10 centimetre strip after 20 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. A small gap means a strong curl. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A green spring onion leaf slit open along its length and pressed flat on a chopping board, with a knife cutting it lengthwise into thin strips beside a ruler.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up slits the hollow leaf open and cuts nine strips, each 10 centimetres long.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers of water and a steel plate in a row, with three green strips in each tumbler and three on the plate, and a spoon of salt beside the second tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Put three strips in plain water, three in salt water and three on a dry plate.

setup.art: A curled green strip lying on a plate with a ruler measuring the straight gap between its two ends.
setup.caption: 3. After 10 and 20 minutes, measure the gap between the two ends of each strip.

flow.do: 1. Cut off the green hollow leaves. 2. Slit each leaf open along its length and press it flat. 3. Cut it lengthwise into strips about as wide as a matchstick. 4. Trim nine strips to 10 centimetres each.
flow.say: This leaf is a hollow tube made of living cells. I am opening it into a flat sheet and cutting strips. Look at both faces of a strip. What differences can you see and feel?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut nine strips. Each is 10 cm long. Look at both faces. Feel both faces.
flow.parent: The outer face is shiny, darker and tough. The inner face is paler, soft and a little slimy. If your leaves are short, use 6 centimetre strips and keep all nine the same.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Curling Strip Test. Here a grown-up cuts a spring onion leaf into nine flat strips.

flow.do: 1. Fill both tumblers with cold water from one jug. 2. Stir 2 heaped teaspoons of salt into one tumbler until it has dissolved. 3. Ask your child for both guesses and the reasons. 4. Write them down.
flow.say: Three strips go in plain water, three in salt water and three stay dry. Which will bend most? Which face will be inside the bend? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which strips will bend most. Guess which face will be inside the bend. Say why. Write it down.

good: Plain water, because the cells will soak up water and swell.
The soft inner face will swell more, so the tough skin ends up inside.
Any guess with a reason is a good guess.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect salt water and plain water to do the same thing.
flow.context: This step of the Curling Strip Test is for guessing. You guess before the strips go into the water.

flow.do: 1. Lay three strips on the dry plate. 2. Drop three strips into the plain water and three into the salt water. 3. Push them under with the spoon. 4. Write down the time.
flow.say: All nine strips start straight, so the gap between the two ends of each strip is 10 centimetres. Now we wait and watch.
flow.kid: Put three strips on the plate. Put three in each tumbler. Push them under. Write the time.
flow.context: This step of the Curling Strip Test starts the test. All nine strips go into their places at the same time.

flow.do: 1. After 10 minutes, lift each strip out with the spoon and lay it on the plate without straightening it. 2. Measure the straight gap between its two ends. 3. Put it back. 4. Do the same after 20 minutes. 5. Work out the mean gap for each place.
flow.say: Do not pull the strips straight. Measure straight across from one end to the other. A small gap means a strong curl. Look at which face is on the inside of the curl.
flow.kid: After 10 minutes, measure the gap between the ends. Put the strips back. Measure again after 20 minutes.

ask.q: What do you notice about the strips in the three places?
good: The ones in plain water have curled, some into rings.
The ones in salt water are limp and nearly straight.
The shiny skin is on the inside of the curl.

flow.parent: While you wait, your child can draw the two faces of a strip. If a strip has curled into more than one full ring, write 0 for the gap and note the number of turns. Most families find the shiny skin on the inside of the curl. If yours curl the other way, write down what you see. Your strips are the evidence. If nothing has curled after 20 minutes, add ice and wait 15 minutes more. Thin strips curl faster than wide ones.
flow.context: This is the main part of the Curling Strip Test. Here you measure how much the strips in plain water, salt water and no water have curled.

flow.do: 1. Ask what will happen if the strips swap places. 2. Move the curled strips from the plain water into the salt water. 3. Rinse the salt-water strips and move them into fresh plain water. 4. Look again after 5 minutes.
flow.say: Now the strips swap tumblers. What do you think will happen to the curled ones in salt water? What will happen to the limp ones in plain water? Why?
flow.kid: Guess what happens if the strips swap. Swap them. Look again after 5 minutes.
flow.parent: The curled strips usually loosen in the salt water within a few minutes. The limp strips usually begin to curl in plain water, though some stay limp if the salt has harmed their cells. Either result is worth writing down.
flow.context: This step of the Curling Strip Test swaps the strips between plain water and salt water, to see if the curl can be undone.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask them to draw one curled strip and mark which face got bigger. 3. Only then read the explanation 'Folding: how flat sheets become tubes' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Nobody bent these strips. So which face of the strip must have grown longer than the other?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. Draw a curled strip. Mark the face that got longer.

ask.q: On a curled strip, which face is longer: the one on the outside of the curl or the one on the inside?
good: The outside face, because it has further to go round.
The soft inner face of the leaf swelled, so it became the longer, outside face.

ask.q: Why did salt water not make the strips curl?
good: The cells could not take in water from salty water.
Salt water pulls water out of cells, so the soft face did not swell.

flow.parent: The soft cells on the inner face take in water and swell. The tough outer skin hardly stretches. One face is now longer than the other, so the strip must curl. In the embryo the cause is different: cells on one face tighten and become narrower. The result is the same kind of bend.

check.q: In the Curling Strip Test, strips of spring onion curled in plain water. What made them curl?
options: The water pushed the strips into a curl
The cells on one face swelled more than those on the other
The strips were trying to become a leaf tube again
check.why: A strip curls when one face becomes longer than the other. The soft inner cells took in water and swelled, and the tough outer skin did not. Choosing 'the water pushed' misses that still water pushes equally on all sides. The salt water was still too, and those strips did not curl.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Curling Strip Test. Here you explain your results and work out which face of the strip got longer.

experiments.title: The Nail Clock: is your body still building, and how fast?
experiments.context: The cells at the base of each nail are dividing all the time, and they push the nail forward. In this experiment you mark a fingernail and a toenail and measure how far each mark moves in four weeks. You find out whether both grow at the same speed.
experiments.question: How many millimetres does your thumbnail grow in four weeks? Does your big toenail grow as fast as your thumbnail?
experiments.predict: Guess how many millimetres your thumbnail will grow in four weeks. Then guess whether the big toenail will grow as fast, faster or slower. Give your reason for each guess.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same person, and measure on the same day each week. Always measure from the edge of the skin at the base of the nail to the bottom edge of the mark, along the middle of the nail. Use the same ruler each time. Paint over the same mark if it fades, and never move it.
results_table: Thumbnail: gap from skin to mark (mm)
Big toenail: gap from skin to mark (mm)

materials.item: nail polish in a dark colour, or a permanent marker
a toothpick, to paint a thin line
a ruler with millimetre marks
a hand lens, if you have one
a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Paint a thin line across the thumbnail and the big toenail, touching the skin at the base. Write down your guesses.
Measure the gap from the skin to each line. Paint over the lines if they have faded.
Measure both gaps for the last time. Draw a line graph and work out the growth in one week.

experiments.record: Write the two gaps in the table each week. On day 29, draw a line graph with the days along the bottom and the gap up the side, one line for each nail. Then write what you guessed, what you measured, and what you think it shows.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: gap from the skin to the mark
example_chart.note: These made-up numbers are for a thumbnail. Your numbers will be different. A toenail's line usually rises about half as steeply.

setup.art: A child's thumb held steady on a table while a toothpick dipped in dark nail polish paints a thin line across the nail right next to the skin at its base.
setup.caption: 1. Paint a thin line across the nail, touching the skin at the base.

setup.art: The same thumbnail some weeks later, with a clear gap of bare nail between the skin and the dark line, and a ruler held along the middle of the nail.
setup.caption: 2. Each week, measure the gap between the skin and the line.

setup.art: A notebook page with a simple line graph that has two rising lines, a steeper one labelled thumbnail and a flatter one labelled big toenail.
setup.caption: 3. After four weeks, draw a line for each nail.

flow.do: 1. Wash and dry one hand and one foot. 2. Dip the toothpick in the nail polish. 3. Paint a thin line across the thumbnail, touching the skin at the base. 4. Do the same on the big toenail. 5. Ask for the guesses and the reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: This line sits where your nail comes out from under the skin. How far will it have moved in four weeks? Will the toenail's line move as far? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Paint a thin line at the base of your thumbnail. Paint one on your big toenail. Guess how far each will move. Say why.

good: I cut my fingernails more often than my toenails, so fingernails must grow faster.
They are the same kind of nail, so they should grow the same.
Any guess with a reason is a good guess.

flow.parent: A line as thin as a pencil line is best. Let it dry fully. A child who bites their nails can still do this, because the mark starts at the base.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Nail Clock. Here you paint a line at the base of a thumbnail and a big toenail, and guess how far each will move.

flow.do: 1. On day 8, hold the ruler along the middle of the thumbnail. 2. Measure from the edge of the skin to the bottom edge of the line. 3. Do the same for the toenail. 4. Write both numbers down. 5. Paint over a faded line without moving it.
flow.say: Measure from where the skin ends to where the paint begins. Is there bare nail below the line now? Where did that new nail come from?
flow.kid: Measure from the skin to the line on each nail. Write both numbers. Paint over the line if it has faded.
flow.parent: After one week the gap on the thumbnail is about 1 millimetre, which is hard to read on a ruler. Estimate to the nearest half millimetre. The toenail's gap may be too small to measure yet.
flow.context: This is the day 8 step of the Nail Clock. Here you measure how far the lines on the thumbnail and the big toenail have moved in one week.

flow.do: 1. On day 15, measure both gaps in the same way. 2. Write them down. 3. Ask your child whether the two nails are keeping pace.
flow.say: Two weeks have passed. Measure both gaps again. Is one line moving faster than the other?
flow.kid: Measure both gaps again. Write them down. Which line is moving faster?
flow.context: This is the day 15 step of the Nail Clock. Here you measure both nails again and compare them.
