flow.do: 1. On day 22, measure both gaps and write them down. 2. Ask your child to guess the day 29 numbers from the pattern so far.
flow.say: Three weeks have passed. Look at your numbers so far. What do you expect next week, and why?
flow.kid: Measure both gaps. Write them down. Guess next week's numbers from the pattern.
flow.context: This is the day 22 step of the Nail Clock. Here you measure again and use the pattern to guess the last result.

flow.do: 1. On day 29, measure both gaps for the last time. 2. Draw the line graph with one line for each nail. 3. Divide each final gap by 4 to get the growth in one week. 4. Ask for the three sentences.
flow.say: Say what you guessed, what you measured, and what you think it shows. The nail you see is made of dead cells. So where is the living part that is doing the building?
flow.kid: Measure both gaps. Draw a line for each nail. Divide each gap by 4. Say what you found.

ask.q: The line moved, but the nail is hard and dead. What pushed it?
good: New cells made at the base, under the skin, pushed the older nail forward.
The living, dividing cells are at the root of the nail.

flow.parent: Most fingernails grow about 3 to 4 millimetres in four weeks, and toenails about half of that. Children's nails often grow a little faster than adults'. Why toenails are slower is not fully known. Ideas include a smaller blood supply to the toes.

check.q: In the Nail Clock, the painted line moved away from the skin over four weeks. What does that show?
options: The paint slid along the nail
New nail is made at the base and pushes the old nail forward
The whole nail stretches like rubber
check.why: The bare nail below the line is new. Cells at the base of the nail divided and pushed the older nail forward. If the nail stretched, the line would get wider. If the paint slid, it would smear.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Nail Clock. Here you take the final measurements, draw the graph and say what the moving line shows.

activities.title: Seams in the Mirror: find the places where you were joined
activities.context: Your body was made by sheets and pieces of cells that grew together and joined. In this activity you look in a mirror for the lines that those joins left on you, before you learn how they were made.

materials.item: a mirror
a torch or a phone light, for looking inside the mouth
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Draw a face and a body outline. Mark every line or groove you found that runs down the middle. Write one thing you wonder about them.

setup.art: A child looking in a wall mirror and pointing at the groove between the nose and the upper lip.
setup.caption: 1. Find the groove between your nose and your upper lip.

setup.art: A child with the mouth wide open in front of a mirror, shining a torch at the roof of the mouth, where a faint line runs from front to back.
setup.caption: 2. Look for a line along the roof of your mouth.

setup.art: A simple outline of a child's body with a dotted line running down the middle from the nose to the navel.
setup.caption: 3. Draw every middle line you found.

flow.do: 1. Stand at the mirror together. 2. Ask your child to find the groove under the nose, and to feel it with a finger. 3. Ask what they notice and what they wonder.
flow.say: Look at the groove between your nose and your lip. Everyone has one. What do you notice about it? Why do you think it is there?
flow.kid: Look in the mirror. Find the groove under your nose. Feel it. Why is it there?

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: It is exactly in the middle.
It has two little ridges, one on each side.
Maybe two halves of my face met there.

flow.parent: Accept every idea. Do not explain yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Seams in the Mirror. Here you find the groove between your nose and your upper lip.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to open wide and shine the torch on the roof of the mouth. 2. Look for a faint line from front to back. 3. Look at the line down the middle of the tongue. 4. Find the navel, and the hollow at the top of the breastbone.
flow.say: Let's look for more lines down your middle. Check the roof of your mouth, your tongue and your tummy.
flow.kid: Shine the torch in your mouth. Find the line on the roof. Find the line on your tongue. Find your navel.
flow.parent: The line on the roof of the mouth is where two shelves of tissue met and joined before birth. The tongue also formed from a left and a right swelling. The navel marks where the body wall closed around the cord.
flow.context: This step of Seams in the Mirror looks for more lines down the middle of your body.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to draw the outline and mark the lines. 2. Ask what all the lines have in common. 3. Then read the intro card together.
flow.say: What do all these lines have in common? What could have happened before you were born to leave them?
flow.kid: Draw your body. Mark each line you found. What do the lines have in common?

check.q: The groove under your nose and the line on the roof of your mouth both run down the middle. What made them?
options: Pieces of the face grew from the sides and joined there
The skin was folded there to save space
They are marks from being born
check.why: The face and the roof of the mouth form from pieces that grow in from the sides and join in the middle. The lines mark the joins. They are there long before birth, so birth did not make them.

flow.context: This is the last step of Seams in the Mirror. Here you draw the lines you found and say what they have in common.

activities.title: Fold a Body from Three Sheets
activities.context: After gastrulation an embryo is a flat disc of three layers. In this activity you stack three sheets of dough and fold them the way an embryo folds. Then you cut across and see a tube inside a tube.

materials.item: chapati dough or any soft dough, in three balls the size of a lemon
turmeric powder, to colour one ball yellow
ragi flour, cocoa or coffee powder, to colour one ball dark
a rolling pin, a pencil and a piece of sewing thread 30 centimetres long

activities.record: Draw the cut face of your dough body. Label the three layers and the two tubes. If you do not want to draw, name them aloud to a grown-up.

setup.art: Three thin oval sheets of dough stacked on a board: a yellow sheet at the bottom, a dark brown sheet in the middle and a plain pale sheet on top.
setup.caption: 1. Stack three sheets: yellow at the bottom, dark in the middle, plain on top.

setup.art: The stack with the middle of the top sheet pinched up into a long ridge by two fingers, and the sides of the whole stack curling down and under.
setup.caption: 2. Pinch a ridge along the top. Then fold both sides down until they meet underneath.

setup.art: A thread held tight in two hands cutting straight down through the folded dough roll, and beside it the cut face showing a small tube on top and a yellow-lined tube in the middle.
setup.caption: 3. Cut across with a thread and look at the cut face.

flow.do: 1. Knead turmeric into one ball and ragi flour or cocoa into another. 2. Roll each ball into an oval sheet about as long as your hand. 3. Stack them: yellow at the bottom, dark in the middle, plain on top.
flow.say: This stack is the embryo in the third week. The plain top sheet is the ectoderm. The dark middle one is the mesoderm. The yellow bottom one is the endoderm.
flow.kid: Colour one ball yellow and one dark. Roll three sheets. Stack them: yellow, dark, plain on top.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fold a Body from Three Sheets. Here you make three sheets of dough for the three germ layers.

flow.do: 1. Ask how this flat stack could become a body with a food tube inside. 2. Let your child try their own way first. 3. Then press a pencil along the middle of the top sheet to make a groove. 4. Pinch the two edges of the groove together over it.
flow.say: A real embryo has no hands to help. How could this flat stack get a tube inside it? Try your idea. Then we will copy what the embryo does.
flow.kid: How can a flat stack get a tube inside? Try your idea. Then press a groove along the top. Pinch its edges together.

ask.q: How could a flat stack get a tube inside it?
good: Roll it up.
Fold the sides round until they meet.

flow.parent: The pinched ridge on top is the neural tube. It does not need to be neat.
flow.context: This step of Fold a Body from Three Sheets makes the neural tube, by pinching a groove in the top sheet closed.

flow.do: 1. Lift the stack. 2. Fold both long sides down and under until they meet along the bottom. 3. Press the edges together, but leave a small gap in the middle. 4. Hold the thread tight and press it straight down through the roll.
flow.say: Now the sides fold down and meet along the belly. Which sheet is on the inside now? Cut across with the thread and look.
flow.kid: Fold both sides down and under. Press the edges together. Cut across with the thread. Look at the cut face.
flow.parent: The yellow sheet now lines a tube in the middle: the gut. The small gap you left underneath stands for the navel, where the cord joins.
flow.context: This step of Fold a Body from Three Sheets folds the sides under to make the gut tube, and cuts across to look inside.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to point to each layer on the cut face. 2. Ask which layer ended up innermost and which outermost. 3. Say where the model is not like a real embryo.
flow.say: Point to the three layers. Which is on the outside now, and which lines the tube? One thing is different in a real embryo. What folded this dough?
flow.kid: Point to the three layers. Which one lines the tube? What folded the dough? What folds a real embryo?

ask.q: What folded the dough, and what folds a real embryo?
good: My hands folded the dough.
In an embryo the cells change shape and move, so the sheet folds itself.

check.q: The sides of a flat, three-layered embryo fold down until they meet. Which layer ends up lining the tube inside?
options: The ectoderm, the outer layer
The mesoderm, the middle layer
The endoderm, the inner layer
check.why: The endoderm is on the underside of the flat embryo. When the sides fold down and under, it is rolled up inside and lines the gut tube. The ectoderm ends up covering the outside.

flow.context: This is the last step of Fold a Body from Three Sheets. Here you name the layers on the cut face and say how the model differs from a real embryo.

activities.title: Body Map: which germ layer made which part of you?
activities.context: Every part of you came from one or more of three germ layers: the ectoderm, the mesoderm and the endoderm. In this activity you guess which parts share a layer, and then colour a map of your body in three colours.

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper
colour pencils or crayons in three colours
a pencil

activities.record: Keep your coloured Body Map. Under it, write the name of one organ that needed all three layers.

setup.art: A simple outline of a child's body drawn on paper, with the brain, heart, lungs, stomach, bones of one arm and a patch of skin sketched in.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a body outline with a few parts inside.

setup.art: The same outline with skin, brain and nerves coloured blue, bones, muscles and heart coloured red, and food tube, liver and lungs coloured yellow.
setup.caption: 2. Colour each part by the layer that made it.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a body outline. 2. They draw in the brain, a nerve, the heart, a bone, a muscle, the stomach, the liver and the lungs. 3. Ask which parts they think came from the same layer, and why.
flow.say: Three layers made all of this. Which parts do you think came from the same layer? What is your reason?
flow.kid: Draw a body. Add brain, heart, bone, muscle, stomach, liver and lungs. Guess which parts share a layer.
flow.parent: Most children group by job: brain with heart, or skin with muscle. Write the guess down and do not correct it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Body Map. Here you draw the body and guess which parts came from the same germ layer.

flow.do: 1. Read out the list. Outer layer: outer skin, hair, nails, brain, spinal cord, nerves. Middle layer: bones, muscles, heart, blood, kidneys. Inner layer: lining of the food tube, liver, lining of the lungs. 2. Your child colours each part.
flow.say: Here is what scientists found by following the cells. Colour the outer layer's parts in one colour, the middle layer's in a second, and the inner layer's in a third.
flow.kid: Listen to the list. Colour each part in the colour of the layer that made it.
flow.context: This step of Body Map colours each body part by the germ layer that made it.

flow.do: 1. Compare the map with the first guess. 2. Ask what surprised your child. 3. Ask them to colour the stomach again: yellow lining, red muscle wall and a blue nerve.
flow.say: What surprised you? Your brain and your skin are the same colour. What does that tell you about where the brain's cells began?
flow.kid: What surprised you? Now colour the stomach in all three colours: lining, muscle and nerve.

ask.q: Brain and skin come from the same layer. What does that tell you?
good: The brain started on the outside of the embryo.
The brain is a piece of the outer sheet that folded inwards.

check.q: Which two body parts came from the same germ layer?
options: Brain and fingernail
Brain and heart
Stomach lining and bone
check.why: The brain and the nails both come from the ectoderm, the outer layer. The heart and bones come from the mesoderm, and the stomach lining from the endoderm. Choosing 'brain and heart' groups parts by how important they feel, not by where their cells began.

flow.context: This is the last step of Body Map. Here you compare the map with your guess, and colour one organ made by all three layers.

activities.title: The Mirror Wing: how does a finger know which finger to be?
activities.context: A growing hand has a small group of cells at its little-finger edge that sends out a signal. In this activity a coin stands for those cells. You count how far each finger place is from the coin, and find out what happens when a second coin is added at the other edge.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
coins of the same kind

activities.record: Draw the three hands you made: with one coin, with two coins, and with a coin in the middle. Write which fingers each hand has.

setup.art: A paddle shape drawn on paper with five empty boxes in a row across it, numbered 1 to 5, and a coin lying just outside box 1.
setup.caption: 1. Draw five boxes in a row. Put a coin beside box 1.

setup.art: The same five boxes with a little finger drawn in box 1, then a ring finger, middle finger, index finger and a thumb in box 5.
setup.caption: 2. Count the steps from the coin. Draw the finger that fits each count.

setup.art: The five boxes with a coin at each end, and the fingers drawn as little, ring, middle, ring, little.
setup.caption: 3. Add a second coin at the other edge, and count from the nearer coin.

flow.do: 1. Draw five boxes in a row and number them 1 to 5. 2. Put one coin beside box 1. 3. Read the rule: a box 1 step from the coin grows a little finger. Then 2 steps gives a ring finger, 3 a middle finger, 4 an index finger and 5 a thumb. 4. Your child draws the five fingers.
flow.say: The coin is a group of cells sending out a signal. The signal gets weaker with every step. Each box senses how strong it is, and builds the finger that fits.
flow.kid: Draw five boxes. Put a coin beside box 1. Count the steps from the coin. Draw the finger for each count.
flow.parent: Box 1 counts as 1 step from the coin. The hand comes out as little, ring, middle, index, thumb.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Mirror Wing. Here a coin stands for the signalling cells, and you draw the finger each box builds.

flow.do: 1. Draw five new boxes. 2. Put one coin beside box 1 and a second coin beside box 5. 3. Ask your child to guess what hand will grow, and why. 4. They count from the nearer coin for each box and draw the fingers.
flow.say: Now there is a second group of signalling cells at the thumb edge. Each box senses the nearer coin. What hand will grow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put a coin at both ends. Guess what hand grows. Say why. Count from the nearer coin. Draw the fingers.

ask.q: What hand grew with two coins?
good: Little, ring, middle, ring, little.
A mirror hand, with no thumb at all.

flow.parent: This is what John Saunders and Mary Gasseling saw in chick wings in 1968. A real wing bud with a second signal also grows wider, so it has room for extra fingers.
flow.context: This step of the Mirror Wing adds a second coin at the thumb edge, to see what hand grows.

flow.do: 1. Draw five more boxes. 2. Ask where the coin should go to make a hand with the little finger in the middle. 3. Test the idea by counting. 4. Ask what a hand with no coin at all would be.
flow.say: Where would you put one coin to get a little finger in the middle? And what if there were no coin at all?
flow.kid: Where must the coin go to put the little finger in the middle? Test it. What if there is no coin?
flow.parent: A coin at box 3 gives middle, ring, little, ring, middle. With no signal at all, real limb buds build very few fingers, and those are thumb-like.

check.q: Cells at the thumb edge of a hand bud sense very little of the Sonic hedgehog signal. Why do they build a thumb?
options: They carry special thumb DNA
A weak signal tells them they are far from the source
The other fingers were already taken
check.why: All the cells in the hand bud carry the same DNA. What differs is how much signal reaches them. A weak signal means 'far from the little-finger edge', and cells there build a thumb.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Mirror Wing. Here you work out where the signal must be to make a different hand.

activities.title: Regrow the Arm: do the cells at a cut know where they are?
activities.context: An axolotl who loses a hand regrows a hand, and one who loses an arm regrows an arm. In this activity a paper strip of numbered boxes stands for her arm. You cut it and regrow it by two different rules, to find out which rule her cells must be following.

materials.item: strips of paper about 3 centimetres wide and 24 centimetres long
scissors, sticky tape and a pencil

activities.safety: Use round-tipped scissors, or ask a grown-up to cut.
activities.record: Tape your regrown strips into your notebook. Next to each, write the rule you used and whether the arm came out right.

setup.art: A long paper strip divided into eight boxes numbered 1 to 8, with 'shoulder' written under box 1 and 'fingertips' under box 8.
setup.caption: 1. Draw eight boxes on a strip. Number them 1 at the shoulder to 8 at the fingertips.

setup.art: The same strip cut after box 5, with a fresh blank piece taped on and the numbers 6, 7 and 8 written on the new piece.
setup.caption: 2. Cut the strip. Tape on new paper and regrow it by the rule.

flow.do: 1. Draw eight boxes on each of three strips and number them 1 to 8. 2. Write 'shoulder' at 1 and 'fingertips' at 8. 3. Cut one strip after box 5 and throw away boxes 6 to 8. 4. Ask what the cells at the cut need to know to regrow the arm correctly.
flow.say: This strip is an axolotl's arm. Box 8 is her fingertips. I have cut it at the wrist. What do the cells at the cut need to know to build the right missing part?
flow.kid: Number three strips 1 to 8. Cut one after box 5. What must the cells at the cut know?

ask.q: What do the cells at the cut need to know?
good: Where they are along the arm.
That they are number 5, so 6, 7 and 8 are missing.

flow.context: This is the first step of Regrow the Arm. Here you make paper arms with numbered boxes and cut the first one.

flow.do: 1. Read rule A: the cells at the cut remember their number, and build the next numbers up to 8. 2. Your child tapes on new paper and writes the new boxes. 3. Cut a second strip after box 2 and regrow it by rule A.
flow.say: Rule A says the cells remember their number. They build the numbers that come after it, up to 8. Regrow both arms by rule A.
flow.kid: Rule A: the cut remembers its number. Build the next numbers up to 8. Do it for both strips.
flow.parent: Both arms come out as 1 to 8, the right length. The wrist cut needed three new boxes and the upper-arm cut needed six.
flow.context: This step of Regrow the Arm regrows two cut strips by rule A, in which the cells at the cut remember their number.

flow.do: 1. Cut the third strip after box 5. 2. Read rule B: the cells at the cut forget their number and start again from 1. 3. Ask your child to guess what the arm will look like. 4. They tape on new paper and write boxes 1 to 8 after the cut.
flow.say: Rule B says the cells at the cut forget where they are and start from the shoulder. What will this arm look like? Why?
flow.kid: Rule B: the cut forgets its number. It starts again from 1. Guess what you will get. Then build it.

ask.q: Which rule do a real axolotl's cells follow, and how do you know?
good: Rule A, because she regrows only the missing part.
Rule B would give a whole extra arm growing from the wrist.

flow.parent: Rule B gives 1 to 5 followed by 1 to 8: a whole arm growing from a wrist. This really happens when a regrowing axolotl is given retinoic acid, which resets the cells' address towards the shoulder.

check.q: An axolotl cut at the wrist regrows only a hand. What does that show about the cells at the cut?
options: They keep a record of where along the arm they are
They copy the hand on the other side
They grow until they run out of food
check.why: The stump builds exactly what is missing, whether the cut is at the wrist or the shoulder. So the cells at the cut must hold a record of their own place. Scientists call it positional memory.

flow.context: This is the last step of Regrow the Arm. Here you regrow a strip by rule B, in which the cells forget their place, and compare the two rules.

activities.title: The Embryo Ruler: how big were you each week?
activities.context: A human embryo grows from one cell to a tiny body with every main organ begun, in eight weeks. In this activity you draw the embryo's real size at seven ages on one strip of paper, and write what was being built at each age.

materials.item: a strip of paper about 5 centimetres wide and 30 centimetres long
a ruler with millimetre marks and a sharp pencil

activities.record: Keep the strip. Circle the week in which you think the most changed, and write one sentence saying why.

setup.art: A paper strip divided into seven boxes labelled Day 1, Day 21, Day 28, Day 35, Day 42, Day 49 and Day 56.
setup.caption: 1. Divide the strip into seven boxes and write the days.

setup.art: The same strip with a short line of the right length drawn in each box, from a tiny dot in the first box to a line 3 centimetres long in the last, and a note under each.
setup.caption: 2. In each box draw a line as long as the embryo was, and write what was being built.

flow.do: 1. Divide the strip into seven boxes. 2. Label them Day 1, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49 and 56. 3. Ask your child to guess how long the embryo is on day 28 and on day 56, and to say why.
flow.say: On day 1 you were one cell, a tenth of a millimetre across. How long do you think you were after four weeks? And after eight weeks?
flow.kid: Make seven boxes. Write the days. Guess your length on day 28 and day 56.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Embryo Ruler. Here you set up the strip and guess how long the embryo is at four and eight weeks.

flow.do: 1. Read out the lengths. Day 1: a dot, 0.1 millimetres. Day 21: 2 millimetres. Day 28: 4 millimetres. Day 35: 8 millimetres. Day 42: 12 millimetres. Day 49: 18 millimetres. Day 56: 30 millimetres. 2. Your child draws a line of each length in its box.
flow.say: These are typical lengths, measured from the top of the head to the bottom. Draw each one as exactly as you can.
flow.kid: Listen to each length. Draw a line that long in its box. Use the millimetre marks.
flow.parent: These are typical values. Real embryos of the same age differ by a millimetre or two.
flow.context: This step of the Embryo Ruler draws the real length of the embryo at seven ages.

flow.do: 1. Read out what is built when. Day 21: three layers, folding begins. Day 28: heart beating, neural tube closed, arm buds. Day 42: hand paddles. Day 56: separate fingers, every main organ begun. 2. Your child writes a short note in each box.
flow.say: Now write what was being built at each age. Which is the bigger surprise: how small you were, or how much was already made?
flow.kid: Write what was being built in each box. What surprises you most?

check.q: A human embryo's heart starts to beat at about day 22. About how long is the whole embryo then?
options: About 3 millimetres
About 3 centimetres
About 30 centimetres
check.why: At three weeks the embryo is about 2 to 3 millimetres long, shorter than a grain of rice. The heart is working long before the body is big enough to see easily. Three centimetres is the length at eight weeks.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Embryo Ruler. Here you write what was being built at each age.

projects.title: My First Eight Weeks: a flip book from one cell to a body
projects.context: No camera filmed your first eight weeks. In this project you draw them as a flip book of 16 pages. When you flick the pages, one cell divides, forms layers, folds, and grows buds and fingers.

materials.item: small sheets of paper all the same size, about 7 centimetres by 10 centimetres (cut from old notebook pages)
a pencil, an eraser and colour pencils
a stapler or a strong clip

schedule.what: Plan the 16 pages in a list, and draw pages 1 to 6: one cell, the divisions and the hollow ball.
Draw pages 7 to 12: the flat disc, the streak, three layers, the folding and the beating heart tube.
Draw pages 13 to 16: buds, hand paddles and fingers. Clip the book, flick it and show it to someone.

projects.record: Keep the flip book. On the back cover, write the day of each page, from day 1 to day 56.

setup.art: Sixteen small paper sheets laid out in four rows on a table, each with a small pencil drawing in the same corner, starting with one circle and ending with a tiny curled embryo with fingers.
setup.caption: 1. Draw one stage on each small page, always in the same corner.

setup.art: A child's thumb flicking through a small stapled booklet, with the drawing in the corner seeming to move.
setup.caption: 2. Clip the pages in order and flick them.

flow.do: 1. Write a list of 16 stages together, using the explanation cards. 2. Your child draws pages 1 to 6 in the bottom right corner of each sheet: 1 cell, 2 cells, 4, 8, a solid ball, a hollow ball. 3. Keep every drawing the same size.
flow.say: Each page changes only a little from the one before. For the first six pages the embryo does not get bigger. Why not?
flow.kid: List 16 stages. Draw pages 1 to 6 in the same corner. Keep the circle the same size.

ask.q: Why does the embryo not get bigger while the cells divide?
good: The embryo is not eating yet.
The cells share out what was in the egg cell, so each is smaller.

flow.context: This is day 1 of My First Eight Weeks. Here you plan the flip book and draw the first cell divisions.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws pages 7 to 12. 2. Page 7: a flat disc. Page 8: a groove at one end. Page 9: three coloured layers. Page 10: the edges of the top layer rising. Page 11: a closed tube and curled sides. Page 12: a small curved body with a heart tube.
flow.say: These pages are weeks three and four. The flat disc gets its layers, and then it folds. Use three colours for the three layers.
flow.kid: Draw pages 7 to 12: disc, groove, three layers, rising edges, closed tube, curved body with a heart.
flow.parent: The drawings can be simple shapes. What matters is that each page follows from the last.
flow.context: This is day 2 of My First Eight Weeks. Here you draw gastrulation and folding.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws pages 13 to 16: arm and leg buds, longer buds, hand paddles, and separate fingers and toes. 2. Stack the pages in order and clip the left edge. 3. Flick the pages. 4. Your child shows it to someone and tells what happens.
flow.say: Flick the book and tell me what happens, in order. At which page does the embryo first have a head end and a tail end?
flow.kid: Draw pages 13 to 16: buds, longer buds, paddles, fingers. Clip the book. Flick it. Tell the story.

check.q: In which order do these happen in a human embryo?
options: Three layers, then folding into tubes, then limb buds
Limb buds, then three layers, then folding
Folding into tubes, then three layers, then limb buds
check.why: The three layers form in week 3. The flat embryo folds into tubes in week 4, and the limb buds appear at the end of week 4. Nothing can fold before there are sheets to fold.

flow.context: This is day 3 of My First Eight Weeks. Here you draw the limbs, clip the flip book and show it.

challenges.title: The One-Sheet Body: make a tube inside a tube without cutting
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A real embryo turns one flat disc into a body with a food tube running through, and never cuts or glues on a new piece. Here you try to do the same with one sheet of paper.
challenges.problem: Start with one flat sheet of paper. Turn it into a closed body with a tube running through the inside, open at both ends, the way your food tube runs from mouth to bottom.
constraints: Use one sheet only. You may not cut it or add a second sheet.
You may use up to six small pieces of sticky tape to hold joins.
The inner tube must be open at both ends, so that a pencil can pass right through.
materials: sheets of A4 paper or old newspaper
a pencil, to test the tube
a colour pencil, to colour one face of the sheet before you start
general: Roll the whole sheet into one tube and tape it. This gives a tube, but not a tube inside a body.
Roll a narrow tube from one edge, then wrap the rest of the sheet loosely round it.
Fold the sheet in half and tape the long edges, to make a flat sleeve.
creative: Colour the underside yellow. Fold both long sides down and under, and tape them where they meet. The yellow face now lines a tube, as the endoderm lines the gut.
Before folding, pleat a ridge along the top, to stand for the neural tube.
Leave a small gap where the sides meet underneath, to stand for the navel.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own. Which face of your sheet ended up inside the tube? Where is the join, and what part of your own body does that join remind you of?

setup.art: A flat sheet of paper on a table with its underside coloured yellow, and a pencil lying beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Start with one flat sheet. Colour one face.

setup.art: The same sheet with both long sides folded down and under and taped where they meet, making a tube with the yellow face inside, and a pencil passing through the tube.
setup.caption: 2. Fold it into a body with a tube inside. Test the tube with a pencil.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the three rules together. 2. Your child colours one face of a sheet. 3. They try their first idea. 4. Test it by passing a pencil through the tube.
flow.say: One flat sheet has to become a body with a tube through it. What is your first idea? Try it.
flow.kid: Read the rules. Colour one face of the sheet. Try your first idea. Push a pencil through.
flow.context: This is the first step of the One-Sheet Body. Here you read the problem and try your first idea.

flow.do: 1. Try one of the usual ways, such as rolling a narrow tube and wrapping the rest around it. 2. Ask what is good and what is poor about it. 3. Then try folding both sides down and under.
flow.say: Here is a usual way. What works, and what does not? Now try the way an embryo does it, with the sides folding under.
flow.kid: Try a usual way. What works? What does not? Now fold both sides down and under.

ask.q: When the sides fold under and meet, which face of the sheet lines the tube?
good: The underside.
The face that was at the bottom, like the endoderm.

flow.context: This step of the One-Sheet Body tries a usual solution and then the embryo's way.

flow.do: 1. Your child designs their own version and says what each fold is for. 2. They build it and test it with the pencil. 3. They find the join and compare it with their own body.
flow.say: Now build your own design. Where is the join on your paper body? Where is the same join on you?
flow.kid: Design your own. Build it. Test it with a pencil. Find the join. Where is that join on you?
flow.parent: On the paper body the join runs along the belly. On a real body the sides met along the front, and the navel is the last place that closed.

check.q: The lining of your food tube is the inside of you. Where was that sheet of cells in the flat embryo?
options: On the underside of the flat disc
In the middle layer of the disc
It grew later, from the mouth inwards
check.why: The endoderm was the bottom face of the flat embryo. When the sides folded down and met, that face was rolled up inside. So the lining of your gut began as an outside surface.

flow.context: This is the last step of the One-Sheet Body. Here you build your own design and find where the sheet joined.

challenges.title: The Rule, Not the Drawing: build a pattern that no rule describes
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. No cell in an embryo holds a drawing of the body. Each cell follows rules about what they sense from their neighbours. Here you write such rules for a row of coins, and a parent follows them exactly, to see whether a body pattern appears.
challenges.problem: Lay 12 coins in a row. Write rules so that the row ends up with a 'head' of 2 coins turned to heads at one end, a 'tail' of 2 coins standing on bottle caps at the other end, and a plain middle. No rule may name a coin's place in the row.
constraints: A rule may speak only about one coin and the coin on each side of it.
No rule may use a number for a place in the row, such as 'coin 3' or 'the last two'.
A grown-up or friend follows your rules exactly, coin by coin, and does nothing the rules do not say.
materials: 12 coins, all tails up to start
a pencil and paper for writing the rules
a small pinch of turmeric or a sticker, to mark a 'signal', and a few grains of rice
general: Write 'make the first two coins heads'. This breaks the rule about naming places.
Tell the follower to copy a drawing of the finished row. This is a blueprint, which cells do not have.
Give each coin a different label before starting. Real cells all start with the same DNA.
creative: Give one end coin a turmeric mark as a signal source. Rule: 'If the coin beside you has a mark, or is heads because of a mark, and you are tails, turn to heads and stop the message.' Count how far the message goes.
Let the message weaken. Give the marked coin 2 grains of rice. A coin that holds rice turns to heads, keeps one grain and passes the rest to the next coin.
Use two signals, one from each end, so that a coin that senses neither knows they are in the middle.
challenges.your_turn: Now write your own rules and hand them to your follower. Did the pattern appear? If one coin is taken out of the middle, do your rules still give a head, a middle and a tail?

setup.art: Twelve coins in a straight row on a table, all tails up, with a small yellow mark on the coin at the left end and a slip of paper with handwritten rules beside the row.
setup.caption: 1. Lay 12 coins in a row. Write rules that mention only a coin and its neighbours.

setup.art: The same row after the rules were followed: two coins at the left end turned to heads, two coins at the right end standing on bottle caps, and plain coins between.
setup.caption: 2. A follower obeys the rules coin by coin. Does a head, middle and tail appear?

flow.do: 1. Lay out the 12 coins, tails up. 2. Read the problem and the three rules of the challenge. 3. Your child writes a first set of rules. 4. Follow them exactly, even if they go wrong.
flow.say: I will be the cells. I can only do what your rules say, and each coin can see only the coins beside it. Write your rules.
flow.kid: Lay 12 coins tails up. Write rules for one coin and its neighbours. Your grown-up follows them exactly.
flow.parent: Follow the rules as literally as you can. If a rule says 'the first coin', say that a coin cannot know it is first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rule, Not the Drawing. Here you write a first set of rules and a follower obeys them exactly.

flow.do: 1. Talk about what went wrong. 2. Try the signal idea: mark one end coin with turmeric as a source. 3. Give that coin 2 grains of rice. 4. A coin that holds rice turns to heads, keeps one grain and passes the rest on.
flow.say: A coin cannot know its place. But it can sense a signal from a neighbour. Let's give one end a signal that gets weaker at each coin.
flow.kid: Mark one end coin. Give it 2 rice grains. A coin with rice turns to heads. It keeps one grain and passes the rest on.

ask.q: How did two coins come to be the head, when no rule said 'two'?
good: The signal ran out after two coins.
How far the signal reaches sets the size of the head.

flow.context: This step of the Rule, Not the Drawing tries a signal that weakens from coin to coin.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes final rules, with a second signal from the other end for the tail. 2. Follow them exactly. 3. Take one coin out of the middle, reset the row and run the rules again. 4. Ask whether the pattern still appears.
flow.say: Now make the whole body: head, middle and tail. Then we take one coin away and run it again. Will your rules still work? Why?
flow.kid: Write rules for head and tail. Run them. Take a middle coin away. Run them again. Does the pattern come back?
flow.parent: Rules based on signals still work with 11 coins or 15. A drawing of 12 coins would not fit. Embryos of different sizes still come out with the right parts for the same reason.

check.q: A row of coins followed only neighbour rules, and a head, a middle and a tail appeared. Where was the pattern stored?
options: In a drawing that the coins copied
In no single place: it came from the rules being followed
In the first coin
check.why: No rule described the whole pattern, and no coin held a picture of it. The pattern appeared when every coin followed the same small rules with different signals reaching them. Bodies are built in this way.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Rule, Not the Drawing. Here you write final rules, then remove a coin to see whether the pattern still forms.

worksheets.title: From one cell to a folded body

items.p: During cleavage the embryo's cells get more numerous. What happens to their size?
items.why: The embryo is not eating yet, so each division shares out what was in the egg cell. More cells from the same material means smaller cells.

items.p: A solid ball of about 16 cells is called a ____.
items.why: Morula is Latin for mulberry, because the ball of cells looks like that fruit.

items.p: Put these events of the first four weeks in order.
a: The cell divides into a ball
items: The cell divides into a ball
items.why: Dividing comes first, because layers need many cells. The layers form in week 3, and the outer layer then rolls into the neural tube in week 4.

items.p: Match each germ layer to its place in the flat embryo.
items.why: Ecto means outer, meso means middle and endo means inner. After folding, the top sheet covers the outside and the bottom sheet lines the gut.

items.p: Sort these body parts by the germ layer that made them.
items.why: The outer layer makes the covering and the nervous system. The middle layer makes what supports and moves the body. The inner layer makes the food tube's lining and the organs that bud from it.

items.p: True or false: a germ layer is a layer of germs that can make you ill.
items.why: False. 'Germ' here means a beginning, as in 'germinate'. A germ layer is a sheet of the embryo's own cells.

items.p: In the Curling Strip Test, which strips of spring onion curled the most?
items.why: In plain water the soft cells on one face take in water and swell, so that face becomes longer and the strip curls. Check this against your own table.

items.p: In the Curling Strip Test, why were three strips used in each place and not one?
items.a: One strip can behave oddly because of how it was cut or which part of the leaf it came from. Three strips, and their mean, show what usually happens.
items.why: A strong answer says that one result can be a fluke, and that repeats let you see the usual result.

items.p: Draw a curled strip from the Curling Strip Test. Label the face that got longer.
items.a: A curved strip with the label 'longer face' on the outside of the curve, and 'shiny skin' on the inside.
items.why: The face on the outside of a curve has further to go round, so it must be the longer one. That is the face whose cells swelled.
items.art: An empty box with a small flat strip drawn at the top as a starting picture.

items.p: How does a flat sheet of embryo cells bend into a groove?
opts: A bone pushes it from below
The cells on both faces shrink equally
Cells on one face become narrower
items.why: A ring of protein threads tightens at the top of each cell, so the cells become wedge-shaped. A row of wedges cannot stay flat.

items.p: The neural tube becomes the brain and the ____ ____.
items.why: The front of the tube swells into the brain. The rest becomes the spinal cord, which runs down inside your backbone.

items.p: True or false: an embryo's heart waits until it has four chambers before it starts to beat.
items.why: False. The heart starts beating at about day 22, when it is a plain tube. It is rebuilt into four chambers while it works.

items.p: Draw a cut-through of a folded embryo as two circles, one inside the other. Label the three layers.
items.why: After folding, the ectoderm covers the outside, the endoderm lines the gut tube, and the mesoderm fills the space between them.
items.art: Two circles, one inside the other, with three blank label lines pointing to the outer circle, the inner circle and the space between.

items.p: Why does an embryo need a working heart when it is only a few millimetres long?
items.a: Food and oxygen can seep from cell to cell only over a very short distance. Once the embryo is thicker than that, blood must carry them, so a pump is needed.
items.why: A strong answer links the size of the embryo to the need to move food and oxygen.

items.p: What do doctors give to women who may become pregnant, to help the neural tube close?
items.why: Folate, a B vitamin, is needed in the first four weeks, when the neural tube closes. Tablets of folic acid lower the risk of a gap in the spine.

items.p: Where in a growing hand is the signal Sonic hedgehog made?
items.why: A small group of cells at the little-finger edge makes the signal. It thins out towards the thumb edge.

items.p: In the Mirror Wing, one coin sits beside box 1. Put the fingers in order from box 1 to box 5.
items.why: The box nearest the coin senses the most signal and builds a little finger. Each step further away builds the next finger, ending with the thumb.

items.p: In the Mirror Wing, a coin sits at each end of five boxes. Draw the hand that grows.
items.a: Five fingers in the order little, ring, middle, ring, little. There is no thumb.
items.why: Each box senses the nearer coin, so the counts are 1, 2, 3, 2, 1. The two halves mirror each other.
items.art: Five empty boxes in a row with a coin drawn at each end.

items.p: True or false: the cells that build your thumb have different DNA from the cells that build your little finger.
items.why: False. Nearly all your cells carry the same DNA. The cells differ in which signals reached them and which genes they switched on.

items.p: A gene that turns many other genes on or off is called a master ____ gene.
items.why: A master switch gene makes a protein that grips DNA and turns other genes on or off, so it can start the building of a whole part.

items.p: On a chromosome, how are the Hox genes arranged?
opts: In the same order as the body parts they mark
items.why: The Hox genes sit in a row, and the order in the row matches the order along the body, from the head end to the tail end.

items.p: Match each changed animal to what happened.
pairs: a Hox gene was off in the third middle segment
Fly with legs on the head
a Hox gene was on in the head
Mouse with ribs on the lower back
Fly with an eye on a wing
Pax6 was switched on in the wing
items.why: In every case a master switch was on or off in the wrong place, and a well-made part grew where it should not.

items.p: A fly with a changed Hox gene has well-made legs on the head. What does 'well-made' tell you?
items.a: The instructions for building a leg were not damaged. Only the instruction about where to build one was wrong. So the Hox gene carries the place, not the leg.
items.why: A strong answer separates the plan for a part from the address for a part.

items.p: Sort each statement: is it about a signal or about a Hox gene?
items: It is released by some cells and sensed by others
It stays switched on inside a cell and marks a place
Changing it can put a rib on a neck bone
items.why: A signal travels between cells and tells them roughly where they are. A Hox gene works inside the cell and keeps a record of the place.

items.p: A human has 39 Hox genes and a fruit fly has 8. How many more does the human have?
items.why: 39 minus 8 is 31. The human set is bigger because the whole row was copied twice in our fish-like ancestors, and some copies were lost.

items.p: Which animal is the odd one out for Hox genes that mark head end from tail end?
items.why: A mouse, a fly and a centipede each have a head end and a tail end marked by a full row of Hox genes. A jellyfish is built in a ring and has only a few Hox-like genes.

items.p: A mouse's Pax6 gene is switched on in a fly's wing. What grows there?
items.why: Pax6 only says 'build an eye here'. The fly's own cells and genes do the building, so the eye is a fly's eye.

items.p: Why were scientists surprised to find the same Hox genes in a fly and a human?
items.a: The two bodies look completely different, so most scientists expected different genes to build them. The same genes mean both inherited them from one ancestor that lived very long ago.
items.why: A strong answer gives the old expectation and says what the shared genes show about ancestry.

items.p: Two students disagree about what DNA is like.

views.who: Nila, a girl in Class 5 (an imagined view)
views.says: DNA is a blueprint. It is a plan of the body, and the cells copy it.

views.who: Ishaan, a boy in Class 5 (an imagined view)
views.says: DNA is more like a recipe. It lists what to make and when, and the shape comes from the making.

items.ask: Whose view fits the evidence in this lesson better? Give two pieces of evidence.
items.a: Answers vary, but the evidence favours the recipe. No stretch of DNA matches a hand. The mouse Pax6 gene gives a fly's eye in a fly. A pattern can appear from rules alone, as in the Rule, Not the Drawing.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence about what genes actually do. Nila is right that the information is passed on in DNA. The disagreement is about what kind of information it is.

items.p: True or false: the same signal, Sonic hedgehog, is used in more than one part of an embryo.
items.why: True. It helps shape the hand, the neural tube, the face and more. Most signals and genes are used in many places.

worksheets.title: Regrowing, remembering and what nobody knows

items.p: Put the steps of an axolotl regrowing a leg in order.
a: Cells near the cut start dividing
The blastema shapes into bones, muscles and toes
items: The blastema shapes into bones, muscles and toes
Cells near the cut start dividing
items.why: The wound is covered within about a day. Under the cover, cells go back to dividing and form the bud called a blastema, which then builds the missing part.

items.p: In an axolotl's blastema, what do old muscle cells become?
items.why: Cells marked with a glowing protein showed that muscle makes muscle. The cells divide again, but they remember which tissue they were.

items.p: In Regrow the Arm, rule B made the cut forget its number. What arm did rule B give, and why?
items.a: Rule B gave boxes 1 to 5 followed by a new 1 to 8: a whole arm growing out of a wrist. The cells at the cut started from the shoulder again because they did not know they were at the wrist.
items.why: A strong answer describes the too-long arm and links it to the lost record of place.

items.p: Tadpoles given extra vitamin A grew legs where a cut tail had been. What had changed?
opts: The address that the stump cells read
The number of cells in the tail
items.why: Retinoic acid, made from vitamin A, is one of the signals for position. Too much of it reset the cells' address, so they built a different part. Their DNA stayed the same.

items.p: Sort these by what usually happens after the part is lost.
items: A deep cut in human skin
items.why: Many animals rebuild lost parts. Mammals such as humans mostly close a deep wound quickly with scar tissue, though antlers show that a mammal can regrow bone.

items.p: A thumbnail grew 3 millimetres in 4 weeks. At that rate, how many weeks does it take to grow 12 millimetres?
items.why: 12 millimetres is 4 times 3 millimetres. So it takes 4 times 4 weeks, which is 16 weeks.

items.p: True or false: a gecko's regrown tail is built the same inside as the first tail.
items.why: False. The new tail has a plain rod of cartilage where the first tail had a row of small bones. Something grows back, but it is not a full rebuild.

items.p: A cell's lasting record of where in the body they are is called positional ____.
items.why: Positional memory is kept as certain genes that stay switched on. It lets a stump rebuild only the missing part.

items.p: Scientists disagree about why humans heal a lost hand with a scar.

views.says: Mammals seal wounds fast with scar tissue, to stop bleeding and infection. The scar blocks the signals that regrowing needs.
Regrowing needs cells that divide freely. In a long-lived animal those cells can turn into cancer, so the body holds them back.

items.ask: Which idea do you find more convincing? What evidence would help to decide between them?
items.a: Answers vary. Useful evidence: whether animals that regrow well get fewer or more cancers, and whether stopping a scar from forming lets a mammal's wound regrow more.
items.why: A strong answer names a test that could tell the two ideas apart. Both ideas could be partly true at once.

items.p: Scientists disagree about where the shape of a body is stored.

views.says: The shape follows step by step from the DNA and the molecules packed into the egg cell. Nothing else is needed.
Cells also hold a pattern in the electrical charges they share. Flatworms made to grow two heads kept doing so, with unchanged DNA.

items.ask: What would you want to test before choosing a side?
items.a: Answers vary. Good tests: whether the two-headed result happens in other animals, and whether the electrical change works only by switching genes on and off.
items.why: A strong answer asks for more evidence and does not just pick the view that sounds more exciting.

items.p: Draw an axolotl's leg cut at the wrist, and the same leg four weeks later. Label the blastema.
items.a: First picture: a leg ending at the wrist with a small cone-shaped bud labelled 'blastema'. Second picture: the leg with a new small hand and toes.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the bud forming on the stump first, and only the missing hand growing back.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, the first labelled 'one week after the cut' and the second 'some weeks later'.

items.p: Which of these is the odd one out, because nothing is rebuilt?
items.why: Skin, nails and liver are rebuilt by dividing cells. Humans make only two sets of teeth, so a lost adult tooth is not replaced.

items.p: Your nails, skin and bones are still being rebuilt. Is 'finished' a good word for a grown body? Explain.
items.a: Answers vary. Many will say no: the same signals that built the embryo keep replacing cells and healing wounds for life, so the building slows down but does not end.
items.why: A strong answer uses an example from the unit, such as the Nail Clock or a healing graze.

items.p: Why can some cancers be treated by blocking an embryo's building signal?
opts: The cancer cells have that signal stuck on
items.why: In some cancers a building signal such as Sonic hedgehog is stuck in the 'on' position, so cells keep dividing. Blocking the signal can slow them.

items.p: Name one thing about building bodies that nobody knows yet. Say why it is hard to find out.
items.a: Examples: how an arm knows when to stop growing, where the body's shape is stored, or why mammals scar. They are hard because many signals act at once inside living tissue, and because human embryos of two to four weeks are almost never seen.
items.why: A strong answer names a real open question from the unit and gives a reason it is hard to study.

quiz.p: Put these stages of a human embryo in order.
quiz.why: The cell divides into a ball. In week 3 the cells form three layers. In week 4 the layers fold into tubes, and then the limb buds appear.

opts: The embryo attaches to the womb
Cells move to form three layers
quiz.why: At gastrulation, cells move through a groove and settle into an outer, a middle and an inner layer. Attaching to the womb happens about a week earlier.

quiz.p: Which germ layer makes the brain and the nerves?
quiz.why: The brain begins as a strip of the outer layer that rolls into a tube. Choosing the middle layer may come from thinking of the brain as being deep inside.

quiz.p: Which pair both come from the mesoderm?
quiz.why: The middle layer makes bones, muscles, the heart and blood. Brain and nails are ectoderm. The liver and the lining of the lungs are endoderm.

quiz.p: A flat strip of cells bends by itself. What must have happened?
opts: One face became longer than the other
quiz.why: A strip curls only when its two faces become different in length. Equal growth makes a strip longer but leaves it flat.

quiz.p: True or false: strips of spring onion curl as much in strong salt water as in plain water.
quiz.why: False. In salt water the cells cannot take in water, so the soft face does not swell and the strip stays limp.

quiz.p: How does a cell in a growing hand find out which finger to build?
opts: From DNA that other cells lack
From the size of the cell
From how much signal reaches the cell
quiz.why: All the cells have the same DNA. A signal made at the little-finger edge thins out across the hand, and each cell acts on how much they sense.

quiz.p: What is the best description of a Hox gene?
opts: The full plan for a leg
A gene found only in flies
A switch that marks a place along the body
A gene that makes cells divide
quiz.why: A Hox gene tells cells where along the body they are, and so which part to build. The plans for the part itself are in many other genes.

quiz.p: A fly grows legs where the antennae should be. What went wrong?
opts: The fly ate the wrong food
A Hox switch was on in the wrong place
quiz.why: The legs are normal, so the leg genes work. A Hox gene that should be off in the head was on there, and gave the cells the wrong address.

quiz.p: Flies and humans use the same family of Hox genes. What is the best explanation?
opts: Both got them from an ancestor they share
Humans got them from eating flies
All genes are the same in all animals
quiz.why: The genes match in their DNA letters and in their order on the chromosome. The simplest explanation is that both animals inherited them from one ancestor, long ago.

quiz.p: An axolotl cut at the elbow regrows a forearm and hand, not a whole arm. Why?
opts: The other arm tells her when to stop
The stump cells remember where they are
quiz.why: The cells at the cut keep a record of their place along the arm, so they build only what lies beyond it. This is called positional memory.

quiz.p: Scientists disagree about why humans cannot regrow a hand. Which is one of their ideas?
opts: Human DNA has no building genes
Fast scarring blocks the regrowing signals
quiz.why: One idea is that mammals close wounds fast with a scar, and scar tissue blocks the signals a blastema needs. Humans do have stem cells and nearly all the genes an axolotl uses.

applications: Doctors give folic acid tablets to women who may become pregnant, because the neural tube closes in the first four weeks. In India, schools and health centres also give weekly iron and folic acid tablets to older girls and boys.
Surgeons repair a cleft lip or a cleft palate, which happens when the pieces of the face or the roof of the mouth do not fully join before birth. About 1 baby in 700 is born with one.

New medicines are tested for harm to embryos before pregnant women may take them. This rule came after thalidomide, a medicine of the late 1950s, stopped the arms and legs of thousands of babies from forming.
An ultrasound scan at about 18 to 20 weeks of pregnancy lets a doctor check that the baby's heart, spine and other organs have formed well.
Scientists grow tiny pieces of gut, kidney or brain tissue in dishes by giving stem cells the same signals, in the same order, that an embryo uses. They use them to test medicines.
Some cancers of the skin are treated with medicines that block the Sonic hedgehog signal, because the cancer cells have that building signal stuck on.
Doctors treat large burns with sheets of skin grown from a small piece of the person's own skin, using the way skin cells divide and spread to cover a wound.

open_questions.q: How does a growing arm know when to stop?
open_questions.why_open: Your two arms grew to the same length without ever being compared. Scientists know some signals that speed up and slow down growth, but not how a part measures its own size.

open_questions.q: Where is the shape of a body stored?
open_questions.why_open: No stretch of DNA is a picture of a body. Most scientists think the shape follows from genes and chemistry. Some think cells also hold it in shared electrical patterns. The tests so far cover only a few kinds of animal.

open_questions.q: Why can an axolotl regrow a leg when a human cannot?
open_questions.why_open: Humans have nearly all the same genes. Scarring, the risk of cancer and the immune system may each play a part, and nobody has yet made a mammal regrow a whole limb.

open_questions.q: What exactly happens in a human embryo between two and four weeks?
open_questions.why_open: This is when the layers form and the body folds, but embryos of this age are almost never seen. Most of what we know comes from mice, chicks and a small number of old human samples.

open_questions.q: Why is the order of Hox genes on the chromosome the same as their order along the body?
open_questions.why_open: Part of the answer is that the DNA opens up for reading from one end of the row to the other, as the body grows from head to tail. Why this arrangement has been kept for over 500 million years is still argued about.

maths.problem: An embryo starts as 1 cell, and the number of cells doubles at each round of division. How many rounds does it take to pass 100 cells?
maths.explain: Double each time: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. That is 7 doublings. After 6 there are only 64, which is fewer than 100. So it takes 7 rounds.
maths.context: This is about the first pages of the flip book My First Eight Weeks, where one cell divides again and again.
maths.why_maths: Doubling shows why an embryo can go from one cell to hundreds within a week.

maths.problem: On the Embryo Ruler, the embryo is 4 millimetres long on day 28 and 30 millimetres long on day 56. How many times as long has the embryo become in those four weeks?
maths.answer: 7 and a half times as long.
maths.explain: Divide the later length by the earlier one: 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5. So the embryo is 7 and a half times as long. If you grew that much in four weeks now, you would be about as tall as a three-storey building.
maths.context: This is about the Embryo Ruler, the paper strip on which you drew the embryo's real length at seven ages.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one length by another shows how fast the embryo grows, which the two lengths alone do not show.

maths.problem: In the Curling Strip Test, the gaps between the ends of three strips in plain water were 2, 4 and 3 centimetres after 20 minutes. What is the mean gap?
maths.explain: Add the three gaps: 2 + 4 + 3 = 9. Divide by the number of strips: 9 ÷ 3 = 3. So the mean gap is 3 centimetres.
maths.context: This is about the Curling Strip Test, where strips of spring onion 10 centimetres long curl in water and you measure the gap between their ends.

chart.title: Made-up example: three strips in plain water after 20 minutes

maths.why_maths: Strips differ a little, so the mean of three tells you more than any one strip.

maths.problem: In the Nail Clock, a thumbnail grew 3.5 millimetres in 28 days. A whole thumbnail is about 14 millimetres long. About how long does it take to grow a whole new thumbnail?
maths.explain: 14 millimetres is 4 times 3.5 millimetres, because 3.5 × 4 = 14. So it takes 4 times 28 days. 28 × 4 = 112 days, and 112 ÷ 7 = 16 weeks. So every bit of your thumbnail is less than about four months old.
maths.context: This is about the Nail Clock, where you paint a line at the base of a nail and measure how far it moves in four weeks.
maths.why_maths: A rate measured over four weeks lets you predict something that would take months to watch.

maths.problem: In the Mirror Wing, imagine seven boxes in a row with a coin at each end. Each box counts steps from the nearer coin. Write the seven counts. What do you notice?
maths.answer: 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1. The row is the same read from either end.
maths.explain: Boxes 1, 2 and 3 are nearer the first coin and count 1, 2, 3. Box 4 is 4 steps from both. Boxes 5, 6 and 7 are nearer the second coin and count 3, 2, 1. The pattern has mirror symmetry about the middle box.
maths.context: This is about the Mirror Wing, where a coin stands for signalling cells and each box builds a finger by its distance from the nearer coin.
maths.why_maths: Writing the counts as a number pattern shows why two signals must give a mirror-image hand.

maths.problem: Our fish-like ancestors had their row of 13 Hox genes copied until there were 4 rows. How many genes is that? Humans now have 39. What fraction was kept?
maths.answer: 52 genes. Humans kept 39 of them, which is three quarters.
maths.explain: 4 rows of 13 is 4 × 13 = 52. Humans have 39, so 52 − 39 = 13 were lost. The fraction kept is 39 out of 52. Divide both by 13 to get 3 out of 4.
maths.context: This is about the Hox genes from the Address Game. Humans have 39 of them, in four rows on four chromosomes.
maths.why_maths: The numbers 39 and 52 are how scientists worked out that whole rows were copied and single genes were lost later.

how_we_found_out.context: This card tells how people found out that very different animals are built with the same master switch genes.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1894 the English scientist William Bateson published a book of oddities: animals with a normal part in the wrong place. He called this homeosis. In 1915 Calvin Bridges found a fruit fly whose balance knobs were partly wings. From the 1940s, Edward Lewis in California bred such flies for over thirty years. In 1978 he showed that a row of genes decides what each segment becomes. Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard and Eric Wieschaus then searched thousands of fly families in Heidelberg, Germany. In 1980 they reported 15 genes that lay out the segments. Still, almost everyone believed that these were fly genes only. The famous biologist Ernst Mayr had written in 1963 that looking for the same genes in distant animals was 'quite futile'. In 1984 the teams of Walter Gehring in Switzerland, and of Matthew Scott and Amy Weiner in the United States, found a short stretch of DNA shared by all the fly's Hox genes. Gehring's team searched other animals for it. It was in worms, frogs, mice and humans. Mayr had been wrong. Lewis, Nüsslein-Volhard and Wieschaus shared the Nobel Prize in 1995.
how_we_found_out.who: William Bateson, Calvin Bridges, Edward Lewis, Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard, Eric Wieschaus, Walter Gehring, William McGinnis, Matthew Scott and Amy Weiner
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Until 1984 most biologists were sure that animals as different as a fly and a human must be built by quite different genes. Finding the same Hox genes in both showed this was wrong.
how_we_found_out.art: A fruit fly with four wings under a magnifying lens on the left, and on the right a strip of DNA with one short stretch shaded and arrows from it to a fly, a frog, a mouse and a child.

roots.context: We have learned how one cell becomes a body by dividing, forming layers, folding, and using signals and switch genes. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Curling Strip Test, nobody bent the strips. Cells on one face swelled, and each strip curled. Your spinal cord rolled up from a flat sheet in a similar way, because its own cells changed shape. A cycle has a maker who stands outside it. In a body, the cells doing the building are the body being built.
deep_truth.habit: We say a body is 'built' or 'made', the words we use for a house or a cycle. Those words bring a builder, a drawing and a pile of parts with them. An embryo has none of these. Nobody stands outside the embryo, no drawing of the body exists, and the embryo is alive and working at every stage.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Curling Strip Test, flat strips of spring onion curled in water with nothing bending them. An embryo's heart beats from about day 22 as a plain tube and keeps beating while it is rebuilt into four chambers. An axolotl regrows a leg from the cells of her own stump.

three.who_am_i: You are not a thing that was finished and then switched on. You are cells that have been building, and being built, without a break since you were one cell.
three.what_is_life: A living body makes itself. Each cell senses their neighbours and acts, and the whole shape comes from all of them acting together.
three.what_is_this_world: The world holds patterns that no one draws. A braid, a body and a row of fingers can all appear from small rules followed in many places at once.

roots.thread: You started as one cell. That one cell became many cells, and the many became different from each other: skin, bone, nerve and blood. Yet they did this by staying in touch, each sensing the others and answering. The cells never stopped being one body. A fly's body and yours are laid out by the same family of genes, handed down from one ancestor. So the many kinds of animal bodies are also one way of building, changed a little at a time.

teachings.teaching: The old physicians argue about which part of an unborn child forms first. One says the head, one the heart, one the navel, one the hands and feet, one the trunk. Dhanvantari answers that all the parts form together, and are at first too fine to be seen, like the parts of a bamboo shoot or of a young mango.
teachings.link: This is the same question this lesson asks, argued in India about two thousand years ago by people with no microscopes. Today's evidence says the parts do appear in an order, and the heart is the first to work. But Dhanvantari was right that the early stages were too small for anyone then to see.

teachings.teaching: A tree too big to put your arms around grows from a tiny shoot. A tower of nine storeys rises from a heap of earth. A journey of a thousand li begins under your feet.
teachings.link: Laozi says that the largest things come from small beginnings by small steps. A body of trillions of cells comes from one cell, by one division and one fold at a time. No single step is large.

teachings.source: Aristotle, Generation of Animals, Book 2, chapter 1 (paraphrased)
teachings.teaching: Aristotle asks whether all the parts of an animal are there from the start, or come into being one after another, like the knitting of a net. He had watched chicks form inside hens' eggs, and he concludes that the parts form one after another.
teachings.link: Aristotle looked instead of only arguing, and the embryos you have read about agree with him. A net is also made by one simple knot repeated, with no knot holding the pattern of the whole net.

science.text: Every part of an animal's body is made after fertilisation, step by step, from cells that at first look alike. No ready-made body lies in the egg cell.
Flies, worms, fish and humans mark their bodies from head to tail with the same family of Hox genes, inherited from one ancestor.
Where the shape of a body is stored is not agreed. It may follow fully from genes and chemistry, or cells may also hold it in shared electrical patterns.

other_view.view: A cell does not sense and choose in any way that needs a mind. Signals lock onto receptors, chains of chemical reactions follow, and genes switch on or off. Words like 'decide' and 'remember' are a handy short way to describe chemistry, and the building of a body needs nothing more than that chemistry.

practice.title: Trace the seam
practice.say: Sit up and close your eyes. Put one finger on the groove under your nose. Slowly move it down over your lips and your chin. Carry on down the middle of your chest to your navel. Your two sides met along this line before you were born. Now rest both hands on your tummy and take three slow breaths. Right now, under your hands, cells are dividing and building. You do not have to tell them how.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Put a finger under your nose. Move it slowly down to your navel. Your two sides met along this line. Rest your hands on your tummy. Take three slow breaths. Your cells are building right now.

ask: Nobody outside you built your body. So who built it?
Your heart was already working while it was still being built. Is there a moment when a person is finished?
No cell holds a picture of you, yet here you are. Where was your shape before your cells made it?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge in this lesson was reasoned through step by step as a family in a city flat would do it. None has yet been tried at home, so please treat times and amounts as a starting point. The Curling Strip Test (in the core path) needs spring onions with firm green leaves. Cooks curl spring onion strips in iced water as a garnish, and the reason given here is the one that science sources give for dandelion stems and celery, which behave the same way. A source that tests spring onion itself was not found. So the parent note says what to do if the strips curl the other way or do not curl in 20 minutes: add ice, wait longer and cut thinner strips. Curling in iced water can take up to half an hour. The swap step may not fully undo the curl. In Fold a Body from Three Sheets the dough must be soft, or the sheets crack when folded. A real human embryo forms the three layers by cells moving through a groove in a flat disc, and the dough only shows the folding that comes afterwards. The Mirror Wing gives a mirror hand of five fingers. A real chick wing with a second signal grows wider and has up to six. The Address Game uses six addresses and one switch for each. Real animals have 8 to 39 Hox genes, and several are on at once. The python and centipede cards are simplified. In Regrow, Half Regrow or Scar? each answer is what usually happens, and the earthworm was left out because kinds of earthworm differ. The Nail Clock runs for 29 days. One week's growth is about a millimetre and is hard to read on a ruler, so the four-week total is what counts. The toenail is included because the difference between a toenail and a fingernail is big enough to see. In the Rule, Not the Drawing, a parent must follow the child's rules literally for the challenge to work. No part needs a garden.
